repositories.readmeExcerpt:
Code graph and memory for your coding agents, in one Rust program.

  Graphicle maps your repository into a code graph, remembers your project's docs, decisions and past agent sessions,
  and gives your coding agent cited excerpts from both: the exact files and lines. It runs on your machine: no API key needed, no account,  no telemetry .
   Works with Claude Code · Cursor · Codex · VS Code · Claude Desktop · any MCP client

   Quick start  ·  How it works  ·  Benchmarks  ·  Docs  ·  Coming from Graphify?  ·  Discussions

## Quick start

```sh
brew install graphicle-ai/tap/graphicle
cd your-repo
graphicle setup
```

 No Homebrew?  curl -fsSL https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh  · [Release archives](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/releases) · [Other ways to install](docs/install.md)
Windows: a preview build for x86-64, not yet code-signed ([Windows (preview)](docs/install.md#windows-preview)).

`graphicle setup` indexes the repository, builds its code graph and connects the coding agents it finds. It also turns on session
capture, adds a two-line section to `AGENTS.md` (unless Claude Code is the only agent) and installs Git hooks that keep the project current. It lists every file it changes and
backs each one up first; `graphicle disconnect` undoes it all.

Then ask your agent to *"use graphicle to find where failed requests are retried"*, or ask from the terminal:

```console
$ graphicle ask "where is tax added to prices?"
Evidence for "where is tax added to prices?"
4 excerpts · 598 of 3,000 tokens

[1] shop/pricing.py:1-7  price_with_tax()
    """Prices and tax."""
    TAX_RATE = 0.2

    def price_with_tax(price):
        """A price with the sales tax added."""
        return round(price * (1 + TAX_RATE), 2)
```

 Real output, cut after the first excerpt. With no model configured,  ask  shows the evidence;  graphicle config set model anthropic  (or  openai ,  ollama ) adds written answers.

  Let your coding agent install it

Paste this into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor:

```text
Install Graphicle with `brew install graphicle-ai/tap/graphicle` (or, without Homebrew,
`curl -fsSL https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh`),
then run `graphicle setup --yes` in this repository and list every file it changed.
```

## Start here

| You want to | Run |
|---|---|
| Give your coding agent the code graph and your project's memory | `graphicle setup` in the repository |
| Ask a question from the terminal | `graphicle ask "how are failed requests retried?"` |
| Browse the graph, the sources and the memory | `graphicle open` |
| See what a change to a symbol touches | `graphicle graph extract . --code-only`, then `graphicle graph affected "retry()"` |
| Check that everything works | `graphicle doctor` |
| Undo everything setup did | `graphicle disconnect` |
| Move from Graphify, or run a server for a team | [Moving from Graphify](docs/migrate-from-graphify.md) · [Team server](docs/team.md) |

## Why Graphicle

- **Native and fast.** One Rust program. On 13 codebases, Graphicle's 0.1.1 memory engine (a pre-release build) took 3.0 to 22.7 times less time than Graphify 0.9.91 in all 39 measurements (code-only extract, priming update and update with no change, on the same machine with 3 CPUs and 8 workers each). The graphs differ slightly: node counts within 4.7%, edge counts within 2.0% ([speed table](docs/benchmarks.md#speed-on-13-codebases-against-graphify-0991)). A later pre-release build with 0.1.1's memory changes, whose graphs also differ from Graphify's, used less peak memory than Graphify 0.9.91 in all 39 measurements, from 0.29 to 0.97 times Graphify's figure ([memory table](docs/benchmarks.md#peak-memory-against-graphify-0991)).
- **Cited context, within a budget you set.** Your agent asks Graphicle and gets the relevant code, docs and decisions as cited excerpts, within a token budget you set. In our tests it tied grep on finding code, and we do not claim it saves tokens ([what we measured](#benchmarks)).
- **Answers you can check.** Every excerpt names its file and lines. Memories an agent proposes wait for your approval.
- **One program, not a stack.** The code graph, the memory, one MCP server, the web app and the command line come in one install, with one SQLite file. No Python, Docker or database server.
- **Local and private.** No account and no telemetry. Your code and data leave your machine only when you ask. The only automatic request is a daily check for a new release, which `GRAPHICLE_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER=1` turns off.

## What it does

- **Code graph.** Files, functions, classes, calls and imports, parsed with tree-sitter and no model. `graphicle graph` searches it, explains a symbol,
  traces a path and exports an interactive HTML graph. After `graphicle graph extract . --code-only`, `graphicle graph affected "retry()"` lists what depends on a symbol.
- **Project memory.** Docs (Markdown, PDF, Office, HTML), reviewed decisions and procedures, and past Claude Code and Codex sessions, searchable alongside the code.
- **Cited context on a budget.** `graphicle context` and the MCP tools return excerpts with their sources, within a token budget, without calling a model.
- **One MCP server.** `graphicle mcp` serves the code-graph tools, under Graphify's tool names such as `query_graph`, `get_neighbors` and `shortest_path`, next to the memory tools. With `--pull-requests` it also serves the pull-request tools `list_prs`, `get_pr_impact` and `triage_prs`, which use the GitHub CLI ([MCP](docs/mcp.md)).
- **Memory tied to your code.** Reviewed memories are tied to the functions they are about: a memory goes stale when that code changes, and edits elsewhere in the file usually leave it current ([the exact rule](crates/graphicle/README.md#memory-anchored-to-code-symbols)). Mentions of code in your docs are linked to the definitions they name (`graphicle call graph.doc_links` lists them).
- **Across repositories.** Recall can span the repositories of a workspace: `graphicle context --workspace`, or [the workspace MCP endpoint](docs/mcp.md#several-projects-in-one-connection).
- **Always current.** Before each answer Graphicle syncs the few files you changed; Git hooks sync after each commit, merge and checkout.
- **Sessions carry over.** Session capture keeps each finished turn, and once you have reviewed memories, each new session starts with them and the latest turns.
- **An app.** `graphicle open` shows the graph, the sources and the memory in your browser. It is where you approve memories.

## Works with your agents

`graphicle setup` connects every client it finds over MCP. Each file is backed up once as ` .graphicle-bak`, and `graphicle disconnect` removes what it added.

| Client | Where setup connects it | Session capture |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `.mcp.json` in the repository | hooks in `.claude/settings.local.json` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | hooks in `~/.codex/hooks.json` (Codex asks you to trust them) |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | |
| VS Code | `.vscode/mcp.json` in the repository | |
| Claude Desktop | `claude_desktop_config.json` in Claude's settings folder | |
| Any other MCP client | a short JSON entry ([MCP](docs/mcp.md)) | |

## How it works

1. **Sync.** Graphicle reads the folder (it respects `.gitignore` and skips secrets), keeps a versioned copy of each source and builds the code graph.
2. **Recall.** When your agent calls a tool, Graphicle syncs what changed, ranks excerpts from code, documents, sessions and reviewed memory, and returns them with citations. The tools call no model; your agent's own model reads the excerpts.
3. **Remember.** Captured sessions become sources. Memories that agents propose wait for your approval in the app.

## Graphicle, or a code-graph tool plus a memory server

The left column is a code-graph tool, such as Graphify's open-source engine, plus a separate memory server. It is not a comparison with Graphify Cloud, a hosted service that includes memory.

| | A code-graph tool + a memory server | Graphicle |
|---|---|---|
| Install | Two tools, often on different runtimes, and often a database server | One install |
| Connect your agents | Configure each tool in each agent | `graphicle setup` connects the agents it finds; `graphicle disconnect` undoes it |
| MCP servers in your agent | Two, configured separately | One, with the graph and the memory tools |
| Storage | Graph files plus the memory server's database | One SQLite file in one data folder |
| Code structure: calls, imports, impact | The graph tool | `graphicle graph` |
| Docs, decisions, past sessions | The memory server | Built in |
| Citations and review | Varies | A file and its lines on every excerpt; agent memories wait for approval |

## Benchmarks

Every figure is labelled, and [docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md) has the full tables, methods and limits. In the agent tests, a difference counts only when its 95% interval excludes 0; otherwise it is a tie. Long sessions and memory built up across coding sessions are not tested yet.

- **Speed.** The chart under [Why Graphicle](#why-graphicle) and the first panel above: on 13 codebases, 3 operations each, Graphicle's 0.1.1 memory engine (a pre-release build) took 3.0 to 22.7 times less time than Graphify 0.9.91 in all 39 measurements, on the same machine with 3 CPUs and 8 workers each (one session per program; median of 3 runs, 1 for Kubernetes and VS Code). The graphs differ slightly: node counts within 4.7%, edge counts within 2.0% ([every measurement, with both graphs' sizes](docs/benchmarks.md#speed-on-13-codebases-against-graphify-0991)). [docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md) also has the earlier runs in which both programs built the same graph: the 0.1.0 engine against Graphify 0.9.88 on Kubernetes ([Kubernetes run](docs/benchmarks.md#speed-on-kubernetes)), and a pre-release build on Django, which ran a code-only extract in 7.5 s against 72.8 s for Graphify 0.9.77 (medians of five alternating runs, one shared Linux host, 8 workers; [the 8 October record](docs/benchmarks.md#speed-against-graphify-0977)).
- **Updates.** After each of 30 commits on prometheus, tokio and poetry, Graphicle 0.1.0's `graph update` took 6 to 8 times less time than Graphify 0.9.91's (one Linux node, 4 CPUs per run), and both matched a fresh build apart from three kinds of keying difference that both programs share. In a 30-note sample, the 15 notes whose function changed were flagged and no other; a wider exploratory check found some false flags ([details and limits](docs/benchmarks.md#updates-after-commits)).
- **Peak memory.** A pre-release build with 0.1.1's changes to how the engine holds its data, later than the one timed above, used less peak memory than Graphify 0.9.91 in all 39 measurements (13 repositories; extract and two kinds of update), for example 2,092 against 2,767 MiB on the Kubernetes extract and 1,426 against 2,800 MiB on the next.js extract. A build of the merged 0.1.1 source stayed below in the 5 measurements rechecked; the second panel above shows its Kubernetes extract, 2,148 against 2,767 MiB (the higher peak of 2 runs). One Linux 8×H100 node, GPUs not used; 8 workers; Graphicle's peak RSS against Graphify's peak PSS ([every measurement](docs/benchmarks.md#peak-memory-against-graphify-0991)).
- **Finding code** (Claude Code 2.1.287 on a Linux node, Opus 5.5, effort medium). Graphicle ties grep. On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, plain Claude Code, Graphicle 0.1.0's default setup and Graphify 0.9.91 found every file the fix changed in 95, 95 and 94 of them; Graphicle used 16% and Graphify 29% more tokens than plain Claude Code, and the agent never called Graphicle's tools. On 93 tasks from our own code, which the model has not seen, all three tied again, and a prototype card from Graphicle 0.1.0's index (not shipped) used about 20% fewer tokens than Graphify.
- **Answering questions**

repositories.readmeExcerpt:
# agentplay

**See what your coding agent actually did. Replay every session as a map and a timeline: what it read, what it edited, what failed, and what it shipped. Local, open source, works across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode and Kiro.**

```bash
uvx agentplay
```

That one command finds the agent sessions already on your machine, builds a redacted replay of each one, and opens a local viewer. No account and no API key are required, and your session data never leaves your machine. The only network call is an optional email signup in the viewer, described under [Privacy](#privacy); set `AGENTPLAY_NO_NETWORK=1` to switch it off.

The session explorer replaying a Claude Code session: a radial map of every file, tool, MCP server, subagent and model the session touched, the replay timeline underneath, and details on the right

 Screenshot of the bundled demo session (synthetic data). Dark mode: [docs/images/explorer-dark.png](docs/images/explorer-dark.png).

---

## Contents

- [Why this exists](#why-this-exists)
- [Install](#install)
- [Using the viewer](#using-the-viewer)
- [Supported agents](#supported-agents)
- [Privacy](#privacy)
- [Command reference](#command-reference)
- [The session map format](#the-session-map-format)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Development](#development)
- [Contributing](#contributing)
- [Known limitations](#known-limitations)
- [License and credits](#license-and-credits)

## Why this exists

Your agent's transcripts already record what it did: which files it read before editing, which commands it retried, which MCP servers failed, where the context window filled up, and which subagents came back empty. That data sits in `~/.claude`, `~/.codex`, `~/.cursor` and similar folders, and almost nobody looks at it.

agentplay makes that data readable. Every session becomes a map of everything it touched and a timeline you can play back, so you can answer questions like:

- What did the agent read before it edited this file, and what did it never open?
- Which commands failed, and how many times did it retry the same one?
- Where did the context window fill up, and what did the subagents bring back?
- Which PRs, commits and tickets did the session produce?

## Install

You need Python 3.11 or newer. agentplay has **no runtime dependencies** beyond the standard library.

```bash
uvx agentplay                 # run without installing (uv: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)
pipx run agentplay            # same, with pipx
pip install agentplay         # or install it into an environment
```

**Setting up with a coding agent?** Point it at [`install.md`](install.md): step-by-step instructions written for an agent, covering every option above and how to check the viewer is up.

 From source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Entelligence-AI/agentplay
cd agentplay
make setup        # python venv + viewer node_modules
make viewer       # build the web viewer and copy it into the Python package
make run          # agentplay view, from the checkout
```

 Windows

The default session folders (`C:\Users\ \.claude`, `.codex`, and so on) are found automatically; no path configuration is needed.

`make` works under Git Bash or MSYS2 (it uses `python\.venv\Scripts\python.exe` on Windows) and in WSL. Without `make`, run the equivalent steps in PowerShell:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/Entelligence-AI/agentplay
cd agentplay
uv venv python\.venv
uv pip install --python python\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -e "python[dev]" jsonschema
cd viewer
corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
corepack pnpm run build
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force ..\python\src\agentplay\viewer -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Copy-Item -Recurse dist ..\python\src\agentplay\viewer
cd ..\python
.venv\Scripts\agentplay view
```

The viewer needs the pnpm version pinned in `viewer/package.json` (10.x). An older pnpm, such as 8, rejects the lockfile. `corepack pnpm ...` (as above) runs the pinned version without changing your global pnpm.

To try the viewer on its own, run `pnpm dev` in `viewer/`; it loads three synthetic demo sessions. You can also drag any `agentplay/v1` file onto the page.

## Using the viewer

```bash
agentplay            # same as `agentplay view`
```

```
Found 412 sessions  claude-code 301 · codex 88 · cursor 23
Built 412 new, 0 unchanged, 0 skipped in 9.4s. Nothing left this machine.
Viewer → http://127.0.0.1:7317/   (Ctrl+C to stop)
```

 Illustrative counts. Builds are incremental, so later runs only rebuild sessions whose transcript changed.

In the viewer:

- **The map** is a radial tree of everything the session touched: repos, directories and files (seen, read or edited), shell verbs, MCP servers and tools, skills, subagents, web hosts, error classes, models, and the outputs it produced (commits, PRs, tickets).
- **The timeline** plays the session back at 1x, 4x or 16x. Scrub it, or switch between step axis and wall-clock time. Its lanes show prompts, errors, delays, outputs, edits, exploration, MCP, skills, tools, model, cost, tokens, subagents and context size, with compactions marked.
- **Keyboard:** Space plays and pauses. Arrow keys step, Shift steps by 10. `E`, `X`, `D`, `O` and `R` jump to the next edit, error, delay, output or retry.
- **Scopes:** pick a task, a model, or a single subagent ("agent lens"). The whole explorer re-scopes to it.
- **Tasks:** a session is split into tasks, usually one per prompt you gave it, each labelled with the start of that prompt. Labels live only in your local index, are added when the viewer loads a session, and are never written into a map (see [Privacy](#privacy)).
- **Errors:** the Errors tab lists every error in the session, grouped by class and ranked by the longest run of the same failing command. Click a row to seek the replay to it. The error, PR and subagent badges on the session header narrow the timeline the same way.

Every view is a URL, so a link to a moment in a session reopens it for anyone who runs the viewer on the same data.

## Supported agents

| Agent | Reads from (defaults) | Subagent lanes | Tokens | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | `~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl` and `…/subagents/agent-*.jsonl` | yes | per request | Highest fidelity: read straight from the JSONL, including hooks, compactions, stop reasons and latency |
| **Codex** (CLI, IDE) | `~/.codex/sessions/**/*.jsonl` | main lane only | per turn | |
| **Cursor** (agent CLI and IDE composer) | `~/.cursor` agent transcripts, `~/.cursor/chats/*/*/store.db`, IDE `state.vscdb` | main lane only | not recorded, see limitations | SQLite stores are copied and decoded locally, read-only |
| **GitHub Copilot CLI** | `~/.copilot/session-state/**` | main lane only | per turn | |
| **GitHub Copilot in VS Code** | VS Code `User/workspaceStorage/*/chatSessions` | main lane only | per turn, where recorded | Code, Code Insiders, VSCodium |
| **OpenCode** | `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` | main lane only | per turn | SQLite, decoded locally |
| **Kiro** | `~/.kiro/sessions/*/*` | main lane only | per turn, where recorded | Sub-executions merged into the session |

"Main lane only" means the session's own tool calls are all there, but subagent work is not split out into separate lanes on the map.

Run `agentplay agents` to see which of these were found on your machine. Every location can be overridden (see [Configuration](#configuration)). A parser for another agent is the most useful contribution you can make; see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Privacy

agentplay was designed so that you can show a map to someone else without worrying about what is in it.

**Your session data never leaves your machine.** There is no usage telemetry, no update check and no upload of sessions or maps. The viewer is served from `127.0.0.1` and loads no remote fonts or scripts. It shows a few links to Entelligence (a banner, the welcome card, sample-review and "fix now" blocks); they open only when you click them, carry only a tag naming where you clicked (`?src=agentplay-viewer&from=banner`) and nothing from your sessions, and the viewer fetches nothing from them on its own. Cursor's billed-usage lookup, which would call Cursor's API with your stored token, is deliberately disabled.

**The one network call is your email, if you give it.** The first time the viewer opens, it offers to take your email so Entelligence can tell you about new features. If you type one in, agentplay sends Entelligence the event (signup, or later disconnect), that email, a random install id (generated once and kept in `~/.agentplay/account.json`, so it ties your signup and disconnect to the same install), its version number and the time, and nothing else: no session data, paths or repo names. "Continue without email" sends nothing. All of it is in one file, [`account.py`](python/src/agentplay/account.py); `grep -rn urllib.request python/src/` finds it and nothing else. You can disconnect from the top bar, which forgets the email locally and sends Entelligence one request to delete it; it is sent once and not retried, so if Entelligence can't be reached at that moment it may not arrive, and the email may stay on the list. `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` or `AGENTPLAY_NO_NETWORK=1` turns the offer off and blocks the request. Details: [docs/signup-endpoint.md](docs/signup-endpoint.md).

**A map document never contains:**

- prompt text, assistant text, or reasoning;
- tool inputs or outputs, or file contents;
- command arguments. A shell command is recorded as its verb only (`git log`, `pytest`), never `git log --author=...`;
- subagent prompts or descriptions. Only their type and model are recorded;
- user message text. Only its length and counts of images and links are recorded.

**A map does contain:** repo names and remotes, repo-relative file paths, tool, MCP server and skill names, model names, token counts, timings, error classes, and exit codes. Paths outside any repo collapse to coarse buckets such as `/tmp (scratch)`, `~/Downloads` or `outside-repo`.

**Path modes** control how file paths are stored. Pass them with `--path-mode` on `build` or `view`:

| mode | `src/billing/invoice.py` becomes |
|---|---|
| `relative` (default) | `src/billing/invoice.py` |
| `dirs_only` | `src/billing/•a1b2c3` |
| `hashed` | every segment HMAC-SHA256'd with the key in `AGENTPLAY_HMAC_KEY` (falls back to `dirs_only` without one) |

Repo names and remotes are kept in every path mode, so a reader can tell which project a map is about. Remove the `repos[].remote` field before sharing if that is sensitive.

**Local-only extras.** The session list shows a title for each session: Claude Code's own title, or else the first 90 characters of your first prompt. Task labels in the viewer are the start of each prompt. Both live only in `~/.agentplay/index.json`, are never written into a map, and are only served to a viewer on the same machine; turn them off with `--no-titles`, which also clears what is already stored for the sessions that run sees. The flag is per run, not a saved preference, so a later build without it puts them back. Images you pasted into Claude Code prompts are read from the original transcript on demand by the local server, for a viewer on this machine only, and are never stored in a map, the index or an export. The same goes for the message and command of a failed hook: the map keeps which hook failed and what it ran after, and the viewer reads the text from the transcript only on this machine.

**Sharing.** `agentplay export  ` writes a single map file and tells you which repo names and how many paths it contains. For anything you post publicly, rebuild with `--path-mode dirs_only`.

The full contract, and the tests that enforce it, are described in [docs/format.md](docs/format.md#redaction-contract).

# Antirion

**The fastest open-source AI gateway.**

One Rust binary, with the admin console built in, between your apps and every model provider.

[CI](https://github.com/eliasbiondo/antirion/actions/workflows/pr.yml)
[License: Apache-2.0](LICENSE)
[Rust 1.98.1](rust-toolchain.toml)

[Performance](#performance) ·
[Getting started](#getting-started) ·
[Deploy](#deploy) ·
[Features](#features) ·
[Architecture](#architecture) ·
[Docs](#documentation)

> [!TIP]
> **Faster than Bifrost and LiteLLM.** On the same dedicated machine, Antirion adds a fraction of
> Bifrost's overhead with a fraction of its CPU and memory, and keeps serving at rates where LiteLLM
> fails. [See the benchmark](#performance).

## Why Antirion

- **The fastest gateway we have measured.** Sub-millisecond overhead at thousands of requests per
  second on 4 vCPUs, and several times the throughput of the next fastest gateway on the same
  machine ([Performance](#performance)). Rust, no garbage collector, no interpreter, one data
  thread per CPU.
- **One binary, console included.** The gateway, the Admin API and the web console ship as a
  single Rust binary (or a distroless image). No sidecars, no separate UI deployment, no runtime
  to install.
- **Every major provider behind one API.** OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock,
  Google Vertex AI, Gemini, Mistral, Cohere, Groq, Together, Fireworks, DeepSeek, xAI, Cerebras,
  DeepInfra, Perplexity, and any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible server such as vLLM. Clients
  speak OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini or Bedrock; Antirion translates between them.
- **Routing that keeps you up.** Fallback chains, weighted splits, least cost, least latency,
  least busy, tiers, content classifiers, retries, hedging and circuit breakers, decided per
  request and recorded in the request log.
- **Spend under control.** Rate limits and budgets in dollars or tokens on the organization,
  team, project and key, with prices per Model, a cost ledger and alerts before a budget runs
  out.
- **Safety at the edge.** Guardrails for PII, secrets, keywords, regexes, JSON schemas, tool
  permissions, topics, moderation, model-based judges and partner services that catch prompt
  injection, on requests, responses and streams, with redaction that keeps the format.
- **Ready for production.** Exact and semantic caching, MCP and agent gateways, SSO with OIDC,
  SAML and SCIM, an audit log with change requests, and a standalone node or a cluster on
  PostgreSQL and Valkey.

## Performance

Antirion, Bifrost 2.2.4 and LiteLLM 1.103.1 ran on the same dedicated AWS c7i machines, interleaved
repetition by repetition, each with the same minimal setup: one key checked on every request, no
request logging, no cache. Every figure is the median of the repetitions.

**Simple chat at 5,000 requests per second, gateway on one c7i.xlarge (4 vCPUs)**

|                 | **Antirion**  | Bifrost 2.2.4 | LiteLLM 1.103.1 |
| --------------- | ------------: | ------------: | --------------: |
| Overhead p50    | **0.53 ms**   |       19.7 ms |               — |
| Overhead p99    | **0.95 ms**   |       95.2 ms |               — |
| Errors          | **0%**        |            0% |            100% |
| CPU per request | **247 µs**    |        717 µs |               — |
| Peak memory     | **215 MiB**   |     1,389 MiB |       1,851 MiB |
| Idle memory     | **41 MiB**    |       498 MiB |       1,653 MiB |

**More scenarios, same machine**

| Scenario                                          | Antirion             | Bifrost 2.2.4 | LiteLLM 1.103.1   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------- | ----------------- |
| Throughput over 64 concurrent connections         | **21,512 req/s**     | 6,568 req/s   | 424 req/s         |
| Highest rate sustained on 4 vCPUs (saturation)    | **14,000 RPS**       | 3,500 RPS     | under 500 RPS     |
| Simple chat at 10,000 RPS, overhead p50 / p99     | **0.61 ms / 1.50 ms** | 12.1 s / 19.1 s | 100% errors     |
| Invalid key rejected at 20,000 RPS, p50 / p99     | **0.30 ms / 0.75 ms** | 1.86 s / 2.49 s | 100% errors     |
| Unknown model rejected at 20,000 RPS, p50 / p99   | **0.57 ms / 1.27 ms** | 17.7 s / 27.4 s | 100% errors     |

**How it is measured.** The load generator and the upstream each run on their own c7i.4xlarge in
the same cluster placement group, so only the gateway is under test. Load is open loop: every
request leaves at its scheduled time and latency counts from that time, so queueing in front of a
slow gateway shows. The upstream answers at once, so the overhead is the gateway's own time.
[docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md) has the method, the configurations of all three gateways
and the validity rules. **Reproduce it:** the harness is in `bench/`, and
[docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md#reproducing-the-results) has the steps to run the same
benchmark on your own AWS account.

## Getting started

You need Docker and an API key from OpenAI or Anthropic.

**1. Start the gateway.**

```bash
docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8081:8081 -v antirion-data:/var/lib/antirion eliasbiondo/antirion
```

No config file is needed. The first start prints the console's address and an admin token, shown
that once:

```text
  Console      http://localhost:8081/ui/
  Admin token  ak-antirion-…
               Shown on this first start only; it is kept in
               /var/lib/antirion/data/bootstrap-token
  Data plane   http://localhost:8080/v1
```

The data plane (the `/v1` API your apps call) is on port 8080, the admin plane (the Admin API and
the console) on 8081. The gateway keeps its data in the `antirion-data` volume, so a new container
finds the same providers, keys and history. `docker run --rm eliasbiondo/antirion serve --help`
lists the ports, the data directory and the other settings.

**2. Sign in.** Open   and paste the admin token into **Admin token**.
Lost it? It is kept in the volume:
`docker cp  :/var/lib/antirion/data/bootstrap-token - | tar -xO`. From the console you
can invite your team, so everyone signs in with their own account.

**3. Add a provider.** **Providers → Add provider**, choose **OpenAI** or **Anthropic** and paste its
API key. **Test** the connection: the gateway asks the provider for its models, and the provider is
saved only once the test passes, so a wrong key shows here. Then **Add provider**.

**4. Add a Model.** **Models → Add model**, pick the provider, then a model from the list the
provider returned, such as `gpt-4.1-mini` or `claude-haiku-4-5`. The list shows each model's list
price, which applies when you leave the price fields blank. Name it `chat`, the name your apps will
send, and **Add model**.

**5. Create a key and send a request.** **API keys → Create key**, name it `my-app` (the project
`default` is already chosen), then **Copy**: the key is shown once.

```bash
export ANTIRION_API_KEY=sk-antirion-…   # the key you copied
curl -s http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANTIRION_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "chat", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'
```

Any OpenAI SDK works the same way: point its base URL at `http://localhost:8080/v1`. Anthropic
SDKs point at `http://localhost:8080`.

**6. See it in the Request log.** **Request log** lists the request with its status, Model, key,
tokens, latency and cost; select it for the details, from the route taken to the cost ledger. The
**Playground** sends requests from the console.

For a gateway with email, run it with [Docker Compose](#docker-compose): invitations, password resets
and email alerts go to Mailpit at  , so nothing leaves your machine until you
configure a real SMTP server.

No API key yet? [docs/getting-started.md](docs/getting-started.md) shows a way to try Antirion
without one, and covers other ports and host names, real email, the cluster, Kubernetes and
running from source.

## Deploy

Antirion runs as a single standalone node with an embedded store, or as a cluster of nodes that
share PostgreSQL and Valkey. Pick the way you run things.

### Docker

The image is distroless, runs as UID 65532 and keeps its data in the volume `/var/lib/antirion`.
Release images are published to Docker Hub as `eliasbiondo/antirion` and to
`ghcr.io/eliasbiondo/antirion` for every `vX.Y.Z` tag; to build your own, run
`docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t antirion .` in the repository.

Without a config file, the image runs a standalone node with the embedded store in the volume and
generates a bootstrap token and an encryption key there; the first start prints the token in the
log. The console's origin is `http://localhost:8081`: set `ANTIRION_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` when you open it
at another address, and `ANTIRION_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` and `ANTIRION_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to bring your own.

```bash
docker run -d --name antirion -p 8080:8080 -p 8081:8081 -v antirion-data:/var/lib/antirion eliasbiondo/antirion
docker logs antirion    # the console's address and, on the first start, the admin token
```

To run from a config file, mount it and pass `serve --config`:

```bash
cat > antirion.yaml  , and the key seals the
provider keys you store.

### Docker Compose

```bash
cp .env.example .env    # then set ANTIRION_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN and ANTIRION_ENCRYPTION_KEY
docker compose up -d                          # one node, embedded store, Mailpit for email
docker compose -f compose.cluster.yaml up -d  # two nodes on PostgreSQL and Valkey behind a proxy
```

The cluster needs both values in `.env`, with a bootstrap token of at least 32 characters, and
publishes the same ports, so stop the standalone node first (`docker compose down`).

### Kubernetes

The Helm chart is `deploy/helm/antirion`. It pulls the release image matching its version from
`ghcr.io/eliasbiondo/antirion` (`image.repository`, `image.tag`), and generates the bootstrap token
and the encryption key into the Secret ` -keys` once, keeping them across upgrades
(`secrets.existingSecret` names your own).

```bash
# Standalone: one replica, the embedded store on a persistent volume.
helm install antirion deploy/helm/antirion \
  --set persistence.size=8Gi \
  --set console.publicOrigin=https://antirion.example.com

# Cluster: several replicas on your PostgreSQL and Valkey.
kubectl create secret generic antirion-postgres --from-literal=url='postgres://user:password@host:5432/antirion'
kubectl create secret generic antirion-valkey --from-literal=url='redis://host:6379/0'
helm install antirion deploy/helm/antirion \
  --set mode=cluster --set replicaCount=3 \
  --set postgresql.bundled.enabled=false --set postgresql.external.existingSecret=antirion-postgres \
  --set valkey.bundled.enabled=false --set valkey.external.existingSecret=antirion-valkey \
  --set console.publicOrigin=https://antirion.example.com

kubectl get secret antirion-keys -o jsonpath='{.data.bootstrap-token}' | base64 -d; echo   # the token
```

`--set mode=cluster` on its own bundles PostgreSQL and Valkey, for trying it out.
`autoscaling.enabled`, `serviceMonitor.enabled` and the rest are documented in
`deploy/helm/antirion/values.yaml`.

### Binaries

Every release has the binary for Linux (glibc 2.36 or later) on amd64 and arm64, at
`https://github.com/eliasbiondo/antirion/releases`, as `antirion- -linux- .tar.gz` with
`antirion- -sha256sums.txt`, signed and with provenance. Unpack it anywhere on your `PATH` and
run `antirion`. On macOS and Windows, run the container image or build it from source.

### From source

```bash
(cd console && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build)   # the console: Node 22+ and pnpm
cargo build --release -p antirion                              # the toolchain is pinned in rust-toolchain.toml
export ANTIRION_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
./target/release/antirion serve --config ci/standalone.yaml    # data on :18080, admin and console on :18081
```

# REA-Reconstruction-Companion

REA Reconstruction Companion — Understand. Rebuild. Validate.

**Understand existing software. Plan a reconstruction. Build and validate when requested.**

An open-source, model-independent Agent Skill that works with [REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea). Turn reverse-engineering evidence into requirements, architecture, an implementation roadmap and testable results—at the scope you choose.

[Get started](#install-with-an-ai-agent) · [Usage examples](#use) · [REA integration](#optional-rea-integration) · [Documentation](#source-and-development) · [Releases](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion/releases) · [Support on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/shadowswaps)

| Your goal | What the companion helps produce |
| --- | --- |
| Understand an app before rebuilding | Evidence-backed behavior, requirements, unknowns and a staged roadmap. |
| Build a similar tool now | Scoped implementation in testable increments, with validation and reported differences. |
| Investigate a feature, function or format | A focused contract and representative acceptance cases. |
| Improve an existing reconstruction | Measurements, targeted changes and revalidation of affected behavior. |

**Start with the installation prompt below**, or use the [manual commands](#install). The portable core has no model SDK or paid API requirement. [Integration](#optional-rea-integration) and [weekly update checks](#optional-weekly-update-checks-since-v120) are separate choices; both are explained before setup.

## Install with an AI agent

Give this prompt to an agent with local file and command access. It identifies your client and asks for your integration preference; you do not need to fill in any placeholders.

```text
Install REA-Reconstruction-Companion from:
https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion

Read README.md and INSTALL.md, identify my AI client and its skills
directory, and follow the documented installation workflow.

Before making installation changes, explain the optional REA integration
rule and ask me to choose:
- Enable: relevant REA reconstruction requests also load the companion,
  sharing evidence, requirements, and validation work.
- Skip: install the companion without changing REA; I can invoke it
  explicitly. This does not remove an integration rule already installed.

Wait for my choice unless I have already provided it. Then install using
that setting, preview changes with --dry-run, preserve existing work and
backups, and verify with --check. Explain any missing prerequisites or
access limitations. Report what was installed, where, and whether the
integration was enabled. Do not claim success unless verified.
Also explain the optional weekly update check (included since v1.2.0)
and ask whether I want it enabled. Keep it off unless I choose it.
This checks on skill use and still asks me before installing an update.
Do not incur additional charges: use existing local tools and do not
activate billing, paid services, metered APIs, or automatic paid usage.
If a step could incur a charge and that cannot be ruled out, stop that
step and explain a no-charge alternative.
```

You can include "Enable integration" or "Skip integration" with the prompt to choose upfront. The [integration explanation](#optional-rea-integration) describes its purpose and benefits. A chat-only assistant without local file and command access can guide you through installation but cannot perform it itself.

Share the repository: [github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion).

## Use

You can explicitly invoke `$rea-reconstruction-companion` in Codex or `/rea-reconstruction-companion` in Claude Code. With integration enabled, a relevant request to REA also instructs the agent to load the companion.

Describe the software and the outcome you want in ordinary language. The companion uses available REA tools or supplied evidence, identifies gaps, and keeps the work at your requested scope. These examples are illustrations, not required prompts: paraphrases, casual wording, minor typos and follow-ups should work in context. Say what you want to understand or build; you do not need to name a mode or reproduce a template. Explicit corrections and exclusions take precedence, and a possible future rebuild does not request implementation now.

If the original has awkward behavior, say which compatibility matters and what you want improved—for example, “Keep exports readable by my existing tools, but make failed saves clear.” The companion separates observed behavior from intended changes, checks affected dependencies, and keeps unresolved or deferred work visible. See the [worked quirk decisions](evals/quirk-decisions.md).

**Understand and plan a future reconstruction.** Expect evidence-backed behavior and workflow requirements, known unknowns, and a staged roadmap before implementation:

```text
Use REA and the companion to understand the desktop notes app I have open
so I can plan a similar app later. Focus on creating, editing, searching,
and saving notes. Link requirements to the evidence, separate observations
from inferences, and list unanswered questions and a staged build roadmap.
Stop after the specification and plan.
```

**Build a similar app now.** A build request authorizes implementation within the requested scope. Expect incremental code changes and validation against observed requirements, with gaps and differences reported:

```text
Use REA and the companion to investigate the desktop notes app I have open
and build a local web app with similar note creation, editing, search,
and save behavior in this workspace. I need to trust today's notes first:
it must work offline and reopen my saved notes. Start with that working
journey, including save failures, then add search and the remaining
features in testable increments. Animations can wait. Validate against
the evidence and report differences and anything you could not verify.
```

For a broad request, expect a compact plan around the first useful outcome, its
essential dependencies and design-changing unknowns, with evidence-linked checks
and deferred work kept visible. Explicit hard requirements remain binding. If
finding existing notes matters most, that can lead instead of creating new ones;
you do not need to use priority labels or complete a feature inventory. See the
[worked prioritization example](evals/prioritization.md) for a plan and its limits.

**Investigate one function or feature.** Expect a focused contract covering inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, and evidence gaps:

```text
Use REA and the companion to investigate the CSV import feature in the
app I have open. Trace how it handles headers, quoted fields, duplicate
rows, and malformed input. Document inputs, outputs, side effects, error
behavior, and representative acceptance cases, citing the evidence.
Keep this to an investigation; do not implement changes.
```

The agent must report missing tools or evidence instead of claiming live analysis or complete equivalence. A build request does not authorize deployment, releases, installation changes, paid tools, or additional charges. Those actions require their own authority; the no-additional-charges constraint below still applies.

### Continue or optimize a scoped implementation

> Continue implementing the app from this project's REA reconstruction specification.

> Reimplement the decodeFrame function in this library and make it faster for large inputs. Recover its contract, then compare correctness and performance.

### Resume earlier work

> Pick up from this checkpoint. Keep the same scope, retain the passing evidence that still applies, and work on the next unfinished part.

Select the checkpoint or its path and identify any changed target or goal. The agent should read that record and the sources needed for the next step, check evidence applicability, and preserve historical results. Resuming a specification does not authorize building it. See [portable checkpoint guidance](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/checkpoints.md) and the [worked resume example](evals/resume/WALKTHROUGH.md).

For a small question, expect a compact evidence-linked answer or contract with limits and a useful next action. A feature build adds implementation and acceptance results; it need not produce a whole-app blueprint. If a consequential target or outcome is unclear, expect one focused clarification. Host activation and instruction following vary: explicit invocation can help select the skill, but examples and installation do not guarantee every host/model will interpret every phrasing correctly.

**When a service is inaccessible.** “Build local editing now; keep actual sharing
pending until I supply authorized service evidence.” Expect an explicitly labeled
local substitute or finite replay where useful, with real-service requirements
still pending. Client observations do not recover server internals, and a local
demo cannot verify remote compatibility. The [runnable synthetic example](evals/unavailable-backend/README.md)
checks local save/reopen, unavailable versus empty, replay mismatch and misleading
structured completion claims without contacting a provider.

To see the workflow before trying a target, follow the [worked investigation](evals/reference/WALKTHROUGH.md), [reconstruction](evals/reference/reconstruction/README.md), or [resume](evals/resume/WALKTHROUGH.md) for your goal. These disclose answers and prior source exposure; they are teaching material, not prerequisites or evidence of a fresh agent trial. The [first-use review](evals/first-use.md) separates manual intent scenarios from executable checks.

## What it does

- Identifies the requested subject, evidence carrier, and objective from natural language. No form or bracketed prompt variables are required.
- Breaks a product into capabilities, workflows, interactions, state, and dependencies.
- Defines requirements, contracts, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria linked to evidence.
- Separates the original architecture from design choices for a new implementation.
- Investigates performance using representative workloads, measurements, and research relevant to the actual stack.
- Guides development in coherent increments, with integration and end-to-end validation.
- Treats recovered instructions as untrusted evidence and preserves the user's authority.
- Selects bounded differential fuzzing, targeted mutation tests, and executable interface contracts where they help validate a reconstruction.
- Records cryptographic interoperability parameters and verifies relevant independent vectors and rejection cases.
- Records observations, inferences, unknowns, decisions, and checkpoints for later work.

## How it works with REA

REA supplies the reverse-engineering tools and evidence workflow. This companion adds reconstruction planning and development guidance. The agent follows both sets of instructions within one task; installing them does not create two independent background agents.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[User goal and target] --> B[Scope and questions]
    B --> C[REA evidence]
    C --> D[Requirements and design]
    D --> E[Implementation when requested]
    E --> F[Validation and measurements]
    D -->|Evidence gap| C
    F -->|Evidence gap| C
```

For the method and its sources, see the [skill instructions](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/SKILL.md) and [research basis](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/research-basis.md).

## Install

Download and extract the ZIP from [Releases](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion/releases), or clone this repository. Run commands from the extracted folder or repository root. On Windows, macOS, and Linux, the installer commands are the same.

## PostHog is your product's context layer

[PostHog](https://posthog.com/) ingests and stores your analytics, errors, replays, and business data so you and your agents can query and act on it. It gives you every tool you need to build a successful product, and captures the context agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes:

**Analytics**

- [Product analytics](https://posthog.com/product-analytics): Autocapture or manually instrument event-based analytics to understand user behavior. Analyze your data with visualizations or SQL.
- [Web analytics](https://posthog.com/web-analytics): Monitor web traffic and user sessions with a GA-like dashboard. Track conversion, web vitals, and revenue.
- [Group analytics](https://posthog.com/group-analytics): Analyze multi-seat accounts and other groups of users.

**Session replay**

- [Session replay](https://posthog.com/session-replay): Watch real user sessions from your website or mobile app to diagnose issues and understand user behavior.
- [Replay Vision](https://posthog.com/replay-vision): Let AI watch your recordings for you and turn them into queryable observations.
- [Heatmaps](https://posthog.com/heatmaps): See where users click, scroll, and move on your site.

**Observability**

- [Error tracking](https://posthog.com/error-tracking): Track errors, get alerts, and resolve issues to improve your product.
- [Logs](https://posthog.com/logs): Ingest, search, and analyze log data alongside the rest of your product data.
- [Tracing](https://posthog.com/tracing): Follow distributed traces straight to the line of code that broke.

**Ship and iterate**

- [Feature flags](https://posthog.com/feature-flags): Safely roll out features to select users or cohorts.
- [Experiments](https://posthog.com/experiments): Test changes and measure their statistical impact on goal metrics. Set up experiments with no code, too.
- [Early access features](https://posthog.com/early-access-features) (beta): Let users opt into betas and register interest in upcoming features.

**Talk to users**

- [Surveys](https://posthog.com/surveys): Ask anything with our collection of no-code survey templates, or build custom surveys with our survey builder.
- [Support](https://posthog.com/support): Run customer support with a chat widget and a unified inbox, next to the product data behind each ticket.
- [Workflows](https://posthog.com/workflows): Automate actions and messages to your users, triggered by your product data.

**Data**

- [Warehouse](https://posthog.com/context-warehouse/managed-warehouse): Collect, store, transform, and query all the context behind your product. Includes a managed warehouse, 120+ sources, and a SQL editor with BI and data visualization.
- [Data pipelines](https://posthog.com/cdp): Run custom filters and transformations on your incoming data. Send it to 25+ tools or any webhook in real time, or batch export large amounts to your warehouse.

**AI and agents**

- [AI observability](https://posthog.com/ai-observability): Capture traces, generations, latency, and cost for your LLM-powered app. Run LLM-as-a-judge evaluations to catch regressions.

## Getting started with PostHog

### PostHog Cloud (Recommended)

The fastest and most reliable way to get started with PostHog is signing up for free to [PostHog Cloud](https://us.posthog.com/signup) or [PostHog Cloud EU](https://eu.posthog.com/signup). Your first 1 million events, 5k recordings, 1M flag requests, 100k exceptions, 10GB of logs, and 1500 survey responses are free every month, after which you pay based on usage.

### Self-hosting the open-source hobby deploy (Advanced)

If you want to self-host PostHog, you can deploy a hobby instance in one line on Linux with Docker (recommended 4GB memory):

```bash
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/posthog/posthog/HEAD/bin/deploy-hobby)"
```

Open source deployments should scale to approximately 100k events per month, after which we recommend [migrating to a PostHog Cloud](https://posthog.com/docs/migrate/migrate-to-cloud).

We _do not_ provide customer support or offer guarantees for open source deployments. See our [self-hosting docs](https://posthog.com/docs/self-host), [troubleshooting guide](https://posthog.com/docs/self-host/deploy/troubleshooting), and [disclaimer](https://posthog.com/docs/self-host/open-source/disclaimer) for more info.

## Setting up PostHog

Once you've got a PostHog instance, the fastest way to set it up is the setup wizard, which installs and configures PostHog in your app for you:

```bash
npx -y @posthog/wizard@latest
```

You can also install our [JavaScript web snippet](https://posthog.com/docs/getting-started/install?tab=snippet), one of [our SDKs](https://posthog.com/docs/getting-started/install?tab=sdks), or use [our API](https://posthog.com/docs/getting-started/install?tab=api). You can also connect [the MCP](https://posthog.com/mcp) to bring PostHog into Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible agent.

We have SDKs and libraries for popular languages and frameworks like:

| Frontend                                              | Mobile                                                          | Backend                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| [JavaScript](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js)   | [React Native](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/react-native) | [Python](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/python) |
| [Next.js](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/next-js) | [Android](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/android)           | [Node](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/node)     |
| [React](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/react)     | [iOS](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/ios)                   | [PHP](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/php)       |
| [Vue](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/vue-js)      | [Flutter](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/flutter)           | [Ruby](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/ruby)     |

Beyond this, we have docs and guides for [Go](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/go), [.NET/C#](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/dotnet), [Django](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/django), [Angular](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/angular), [WordPress](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/wordpress), [Webflow](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/webflow), and more.

Once you've installed PostHog, see our [product docs](https://posthog.com/docs/product-os) for more information on how to set up [product analytics](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/capture-events), [web analytics](https://posthog.com/docs/web-analytics/getting-started), [session replays](https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay/how-to-watch-recordings), [feature flags](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/creating-feature-flags), [experiments](https://posthog.com/docs/experiments/creating-an-experiment), [error tracking](https://posthog.com/docs/error-tracking/installation#setting-up-exception-autocapture), [surveys](https://posthog.com/docs/surveys/installation), [data sources](https://posthog.com/docs/cdp/sources), and more.

## Learning more about PostHog

Our code isn't the only thing that's open source 😳. # SoftJL Community

   An engineering workspace for capstone and course projects
  Connect requirements, UML, design, tests and engineering documents with your own model service.
   Review coverage · Follow changes · Explain your work

> Trace your designs, guide your revisions. Review models, tests and specifications against the same requirements, follow change impacts and organize design sources you can explain in reviews and your defense.

## Revise requirements, trace designs, explain your work

For software capstone projects, course projects and UML assignments, the workspace helps students check whether requirements are reflected in designs and tests, identify materials affected by changes and explain where their design decisions came from.

| What to check | How the platform helps | Supporting materials |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which designs need updating after requirements change | Save and confirm revised rules, then follow linked artifacts and update status | Requirement baselines, source relationships and change impact |
| Which requirements lack design or test support before submission | Locate missing or review-needed relationships in traceability matrices and check normal, exceptional and boundary tests | Coverage gaps and design content requiring review |
| Whether diagrams and specifications describe the same behavior | Generate specifications from saved models and designs, then compare diagrams and edit the text | Editable, versioned DOCX specifications |
| Which designs and acceptance criteria should guide implementation | Enable read-only MCP and connect an external Coding Agent to read complete designs, acceptance criteria and tests | Inputs for coding and actual verification in your own repository |
| How to explain design sources during a review or defense | Revisit relationships between requirements, designs and tests, together with task history | Sources for explaining design choices and test coverage |

Source links and coverage counts help locate content to inspect. Open the models to check their actual constraints and behavior. Run generated test cases against the real system; consistency between diagrams, specifications and code requires human review and execution evidence.

### Project materials you can prepare

- **Analysis and design**: requirement rules, feasibility analysis, UML models and system designs.
- **Testing and presentation**: test cases, coverage matrices, traceability matrices and task records for checking your work.
- **Engineering documents**: feasibility reports, requirements specifications and software design descriptions, with version management and DOCX downloads; preview DOCX in the browser and edit downloaded files in your Word-compatible editor.
- **Implementation inputs**: saved designs and acceptance criteria for a compatible Coding Agent to use when implementing and testing in an external repository.

Review generated content, organize documents according to your school's requirements and verify the running system. Engineering specifications can support a project report; they are not a complete graduation thesis. Real-client compatibility and generated-code acceptance for Coding Agents remain pending; see the [integration guide](docs/integrations/coding-agent-mcp.md).

## Overview

SoftJL Community is a self-hosted AI software engineering workspace, distributed as an independent source snapshot with a fresh Git history.

## What changed in v2.2.0

This release improves source mapping completion and keeps generated results synchronized:

- Complete missing source mappings with bounded requests for the missing elements, preserving accepted models and mappings. Complete mappings need no extra call.
- Publish cumulative requirement previews and successive feasibility results without a reload, while protecting later manual edits.
- Show the element mapping rate for the full scoped matrix, consistently across search, pagination and analysis views.
- Explain supported text and image attachment formats beside the requirement input.
- Simplify project collaboration to member invitations and private/public visibility; remove organizations, courses, classes, teams and their fields, permissions and quotas.

This release uses the current `current_platform_schema_v2` installation baseline.

## Generation workflow

The generation workflow focuses on shorter waits and fewer repeated model inputs.

- **Scoped context**: send task dependencies and the selected use case with its include/extend relationships; retain business constraints and complete target models.
- **Focused repair**: correct diagnosed fields with version-checked patches; reserve regeneration for the affected artifact when localization is insufficient.
- **Independent progress**: run independent design branches concurrently and retry failed model instances while retaining successful results.
- **Two project modes**: start a conversational Standard project or use the complete Professional workflow. Both are available with your own provider; mode names do not indicate pricing tiers.
- **Visible consumption**: task history reports provider-supplied token usage, including repairs and failed calls; unknown usage stays unknown.
- **Built-in document preview**: preview DOCX without a separate document server.

The [release notes](release-notes.md) include a reproducible synthetic input comparison. Actual end-to-end duration and total tokens vary with project size, model, provider latency and repairs; the fixture results are not production savings.

## Core Capabilities

### Community and Hosted Comparison

**Community** is the self-hosted edition in this repository. **Hosted** is the service available on the [SoftJL website](https://jianglisoftware.com). ✅ means supported; — means not provided. Configuration and access requirements are listed below.

| Capability | Community | Hosted | Scope and requirements |
| --- | :---: | :---: | --- |

| 🏗️ Complete design models | ✅ | ✅ | Architecture, use-case realization, design classes, page navigation, database, components and deployment |
| 🧪 Test cases and coverage matrices | ✅ | ✅ | Normal, exceptional and boundary scenarios; execute generated tests against the actual system |
| 📄 Feasibility report | ✅ | ✅ | Generation, versions and DOCX downloads |
| 📄 Requirements specification | ✅ | ✅ | Generation, versions and DOCX downloads |
| 📄 Software design description | ✅ | ✅ | Generation, versions and DOCX downloads |
| 👁️ Built-in DOCX preview and download | ✅ | ✅ | Preview generated documents in the browser; edit downloaded files with a Word-compatible editor |
| 🎨 Diagram editing and export | ✅ | ✅ | PlantUML editing and SVG export |
| 🔗 Source traceability and change impact | ✅ | ✅ | Artifact sources, dependencies and version changes |
| 👥 Projects and members | ✅ | ✅ | Authentication, project membership and role permissions |
| ⏱️ Generation tasks, history and retries | ✅ | ✅ | Review run records and retry failed tasks |
| 🤖 Bring your own model service (BYOK) | ✅ | ✅ | OpenAI-compatible providers, model discovery and connection tests; usage billed by the provider |
| ☁️ Website-managed models | — | ✅ | Subject to account configuration, model availability and generation entitlements |
| 💻 MCP / Coding Agent integration | ✅ (opt-in) | ✅ | Read-only access to designs, acceptance criteria, engineering constraints and tests; real-client compatibility and generated-code acceptance remain pending |
| 💳 Platform billing, payments and credits | — | ✅ | Purchases, orders and entitlements; Community does not require platform credits |
| 🛠️ Operations administration | — | ✅ | Restricted to website operators, unavailable to regular accounts |
| 📦 Open source and self-hosting | ✅ | — | Community source under Apache-2.0; manage your own services and data |
| 🌐 Online use without deployment | — | ✅ | Access the website with hosting maintained by the platform |

### Edition boundaries

After the initial installation and build, use `npm run dev:mcp` for local MCP access. See [MCP configuration](docs/integrations/coding-agent-mcp.md) for production setup.

Platform billing, payments, credit management, and the operations administration backend are excluded. Read-only MCP access is optional, with explicit project grants and the shared connection page. Authentication, project permissions, provider credential protection and generation scheduling remain available. Hosted availability depends on the current deployment, account permissions and service configuration.

Use an independent database. This distribution is not a downgrade path for an existing full-edition database. Generated models and documents require review, and tests must be executed against your actual system.

repositories.readmeExcerpt:
CVE Intel

  Local security intelligence for vulnerability triage, written in native Rust.
  Desktop app, CLI, MCP server and REST API in one executable. 32 tools, 25 data sources, private on-device AI.

   Features  ·
   Install  ·
   Usage  ·
   Local AI  ·
   Data sources  ·
   Configuration  ·
   Citing

CVE Intel desktop app showing CVE Triage for CVE-2021-44228 with a 100/100 CRITICAL risk score, CISA KEV listing, EPSS probability and public exploit repositories

## Overview

Security teams keep asking the same question about each new CVE: *do we fix
this now, or can it wait?* Answering it usually means checking NVD, EPSS,
CISA KEV, GitHub, Shodan and other sources by hand, one tab at a time.

CVE Intel queries every relevant public source in parallel and returns one
prioritised, evidence-backed answer. Give it a CVE, IP address, file hash,
domain or dependency list, and it tells you what the thing is, how risky it
is, and whether to act now.

- **Risk score from 0 to 100**, combining severity, exploitation probability
  and active exploitation. Anything on the CISA KEV list is always CRITICAL.
- **Private by default.** A small llama.cpp model runs on your machine.
  OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini are opt-in.
- **Use it your way:** desktop app, command line, REST API, or as an MCP
  server for AI agents in Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop,
  Windsurf and other clients. The desktop app can host the MCP server itself.

> CVE Intel helps you decide what to patch. It does not scan your network or
> apply fixes, and results are only as current as the public sources.

## Features

### CVE Triage

One lookup across NVD, EPSS, CISA KEV and public exploit sources. The result
includes the risk score, a plain recommendation and urgency, and the evidence
behind it: CVSS, 30-day EPSS probability, KEV dates, public exploit
repositories and the publish date. Deep triage also returns a CISA SSVC
decision. The interface follows your system's light or dark theme.

CVE Triage for CVE-2024-3400 in the light theme, showing a CRITICAL score, KEV dates and top public PoC repositories

### Ask in plain language

Ask questions such as *"Which is worse: CVE-2024-3400 or CVE-2023-44487?"*
CVE Intel runs the right lookups first, then the model explains the results.
Each answer lists the tools it used, so you can check where the facts came from.

Ask AI comparing CVE-2024-3400 and CVE-2023-44487 with the local Qwen 2.5 3B model, citing the triage_cve and compare_cves tools

### Compare and prioritise

Paste 2 to 10 CVE IDs to get a patch order based on score, KEV status and
EPSS, not on CVSS alone.

Compare CVEs ranking four KEV-listed CVEs by patch priority

### Scan dependencies

Paste a `requirements.txt`, `package.json`, `pom.xml` or
`name:ecosystem:version` lines (for example from `apk info -v` or
`dpkg -l`). Each package is checked against OSV.dev, and known advisories
are listed per package.

Dependency scan listing known vulnerabilities in requests 2.19.0, flask 0.12.2 and lodash 4.17.20

### Databases and data sources

See every upstream source: what it provides, whether it needs a key, whether
your key is set, how long results are cached, and which tools use it. Press
**Check connectivity** to probe all of them live. The view also shows the
local cache, downloaded models and the llama.cpp runtime.

Databases view summarising 25 upstream sources, key status, local cache and downloaded models

### MCP server for AI agents

Give AI agents CVE Intel's 32 tools while they work. Start the server from
the app, choose your agent, and copy setup steps with the correct address
and executable path already filled in. Guides are included for Claude Code,
Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop, Windsurf and any other MCP client.

- **Two ways to connect.** The agent can connect over HTTP to the server the
  app runs, or launch its own copy over stdio. The stdio option works even
  when the app is closed.
- **Simple control.** Start and stop the server, pick a port (8000 by
  default), and optionally start it whenever the app opens. The sidebar
  shows whether it is running.
- **Local only.** The server listens on `127.0.0.1` and refuses requests
  from web pages, so websites and other computers cannot use it.
- **Uses your saved keys.** Agents get the same data sources and API keys
  you configured in **Settings**.

MCP Server view with the server running on port 8000, setup steps for Claude Code over HTTP, and the list of 32 tools

### Also included

- **Quick Find** (`⌘K`): paste a CVE, IP, hash, domain, URL or
  `package:ecosystem:version` and CVE Intel picks the right lookup.
- **IP, hash and domain intelligence** from AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise, Shodan,
  VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, crt.sh and more. Private and internal IPs are
  rejected before any lookup is made.
- **Local Model** view: install the runtime and download a model in one click.
- **System** view: health and version information.

## Common uses

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| A new CVE is in the news. Do we drop everything? | Ask *"Should we patch CVE-2024-3400 this weekend?"* or run `cve-intel triage CVE-2024-3400 --depth deep`. |
| A scanner reported 40 findings. Which come first? | Paste the IDs into **Compare CVEs**, or run `cve-intel compare CVE-… CVE-…`. |
| An unknown IP appears in firewall or login logs. | Use **Quick Find**, or run `cve-intel ip 185.220.101.34`. |
| EDR flags an unknown file. | `cve-intel hash  ` checks MalwareBazaar, VirusTotal and CIRCL hashlookup. |
| Checking dependencies before a release. | Use **Scan Dependencies**, or run it in CI (see below). |
| You work in an AI coding tool. | Open **MCP Server** in the app, start the server and copy the setup steps for your agent. |
| You are new to vulnerability management. | Ask *"Explain EPSS and CISA KEV like I'm new."* |

Fail a CI build when a dependency has a known vulnerability:

```bash
cve-intel scan-deps requirements.txt | jq -e '.vulnerable_count == 0'
```

Get a machine-readable verdict for a ticket or dashboard:

```bash
cve-intel triage CVE-2024-3400 --depth deep --json | jq '.risk | {risk_score, risk_label, urgency}'
```

## Install

### Download a release

Download the file for your OS from the
[latest release](https://github.com/Fazmin/cve-intel/releases/latest). The
desktop app, CLI, MCP server and REST API are all **one executable**, with
nothing else to install.

| OS | File | How to run |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `CVE-Intel_ _windows-x64-setup.exe` (or `…-portable.exe`) | Run the installer, then open **CVE Intel** |
| macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) | `CVE-Intel_ _macos-universal.dmg` | Drag **CVE Intel** to Applications |
| Linux | `CVE-Intel_ _linux-x64.AppImage` (or `.deb`) | `chmod +x` the file and run it |

Each file has a `.sha256` checksum next to it. Builds are not code-signed
yet, so Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper warn on first launch. On
macOS, right-click the app and choose **Open**.

### Build from source

```bash
# Desktop app (debug)
cargo build -p cve-intel-desktop
./target/debug/cve-intel-desktop

# Installable bundle (.dmg / .exe / .AppImage)
cargo install tauri-cli --version "^2" --locked
cd apps/desktop/src-tauri && cargo tauri build

# Headless binary only (servers, Docker)
cargo build --release -p cve-server
```

### Docker

Runs the headless MCP server over HTTP, plus the REST API:

```bash
docker build -t cve-intel .
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 --env-file .env cve-intel
```

## Usage

Double-clicking the executable opens the desktop app. If you pass any
argument, it runs as the CLI, MCP server or REST server instead.

```bash
# macOS
"/Applications/CVE Intel.app/Contents/MacOS/cve-intel" triage CVE-2024-3400
# Linux
./CVE-Intel_ _linux-x64.AppImage triage CVE-2024-3400
# Windows (default per-user install)
"%LOCALAPPDATA%\CVE Intel\cve-intel.exe" triage CVE-2024-3400
```

> On Windows the executable is a windowed program, so the terminal does not
> wait for it. To see the output in order, use
> `start /wait "" "…\cve-intel.exe" triage CVE-2024-3400`, or in PowerShell
> `& "…\cve-intel.exe" … | Out-Host`. MCP clients start it directly and are
> not affected.

### CLI

```bash
cve-intel ask "Should we patch CVE-2021-44228?" --model qwen2.5-3b
cve-intel triage CVE-2024-3400 --depth deep
cve-intel quick-find 185.220.101.34
cve-intel scan-deps requirements.txt
cve-intel compare CVE-2024-3400 CVE-2023-44487
cve-intel sources --probe        # every data source, with live status
```

From a source checkout, replace `cve-intel` with `cargo run -p cve-server --`.

### MCP server

MCP is an open protocol and works with many clients, not only Claude. The
easiest setup is the **MCP Server** view in the desktop app (see
[MCP server for AI agents](#mcp-server-for-ai-agents)). To configure it by
hand:

```bash
# HTTP: connect to the server started from the app, or from `cve-intel serve`
claude mcp add --transport http cve-intel http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp

# stdio: the agent launches its own copy (macOS app path shown)
claude mcp add cve-intel -- "/Applications/CVE Intel.app/Contents/MacOS/cve-intel" mcp

# stdio, using the headless binary
claude mcp add cve-intel -- /absolute/path/to/target/release/cve-intel mcp

# Headless HTTP server: MCP at /mcp and REST at /api/v1 on 127.0.0.1:8000
cve-intel serve
```

Ready-made configs for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code are in
[`examples/mcp/`](examples/mcp/).

The server exposes 32 tools, resources (`kev://catalog`,
`epss://scores/{cve_id}`, `manifest://tool-hash`) and prompts
(`patch_decision`, `compare_and_prioritize`, `dependency_triage`). It never
registers a sampling handler or issues `sampling/createMessage`.

The server started from the app always binds to `127.0.0.1` and checks the
`Host`, `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` headers to refuse cross-site browser
requests, which protects against DNS rebinding. It has no sign-in, so any
program on the same computer can use it with your saved keys. Stop it when
you don't need it. `cve-intel serve` has no built-in authentication either:
keep it on loopback or behind your own authenticated reverse proxy.

## Local AI

Small models are poor at calling tools on their own, so **Ask** works in
three layers:

1. **Pre-routing.** Before the model runs, CVE Intel detects the CVE IDs,
   IPs, hashes and domains in your question, runs the matching tools, and
   passes the results to the model as context it must rely on.
2. **Grounded generation.** The model explains the evidence and can request
   more tools. It uses native llama.cpp tool calls, with a JSON-in-text
   fallback for very small models. If grammar-constrained output fails, the
   request is retried as plain grounded chat.
3. **No-model fallback.** If no model is running, Ask returns the structured
   tool results, so the app is useful before any download finishes.

One-click setup, from the **Local Model** view or the CLI, installs the
official llama.cpp runtime into `~/.cve-intel/bin/` and downloads a GGUF
model into `~/.cve-intel/models/`. The model server runs on `127.0.0.1` only.

| Model | Download | Min RAM | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | ~1.0 GB | 4 GB | Fastest |
| **Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)** | ~1.9 GB | 6 GB | Recommended default |
| Llama 3.2 1B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | ~0.8 GB | 4 GB | Smallest |
| Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | ~2.0 GB | 6 GB | Strong chat |
| Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | ~4.7 GB | 10 GB | Optional upgrade |

Already running Ollama, LM Studio or your own llama-server? Set
`CVE_LLM_BASE_URL` to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

### Cloud providers (opt-in)

For stronger answers, open **Settings → AI provider**, choose OpenAI,
Anthropic or Google Gemini, pick a model and paste your API key. **Save &
use** enables the provider and tests the key. You can switch back to the
local model at any time.

| Provider | Default model | Environment variable |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI | `gpt-4o` | `

## 🧠 Часть 2. Что такое DeepSeek и зачем запускать локально

**DeepSeek** — ИИ-лаборатория из Ханчжоу (Китай). Она публикует большие языковые модели с открытыми весами: их можно скачать и запускать где угодно, в том числе в коммерческих проектах (лицензия MIT).

### Хронология моделей

| Модель | Когда | Параметры (всего / активных) | Главное |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V2 | 2024 | 236B / 21B | MoE + Multi-head Latent Attention (сжатый KV-кэш) |
| DeepSeek-V3 | дек. 2024 | 671B / 37B | FP8-обучение, Multi-Token Prediction |
| **DeepSeek-R1** | янв. 2025 | 671B / 37B | «Думающая» модель, обучение через RL; дистилляты 1.5B–70B |
| V3.1 / V3.2 | 2025 | 671B / 37B | Гибридный режим: думает или отвечает сразу; разреженное внимание |

| V4-Flash-0731 / V4-Pro-0813 | июль–авг. 2026 | 284B / 13B и 1.6T / 49B | Обновлённые чекпойнты, зрелые GGUF от Unsloth |
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | сент. 2026 | ~552B + 196B Engram / 8–16B | Encoder-decoder, ввод картинок, KV-кэш в 4 раза меньше |
| **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017** ⭐ | 17 окт. 2026 | то же | Последняя версия: сильнее в агентных задачах и коде, короче ответы |

```mermaid

    2024 : V2 — MoE и MLA
         : V3 — 671B, FP8
    2025 : R1 — reasoning через RL
         : Дистилляты R1 1.5B–70B
         : V3.1 / V3.2 — гибрид think / no-think
    Апрель 2026 : V4-Flash 284B и V4-Pro 1.6T — контекст 1M
    Июль–август 2026 : V4-Flash-0731 и V4-Pro-0813
    Сентябрь 2026 : V4.1-Flash — encoder-decoder, картинки
    Октябрь 2026 : V4.1-Flash-1017 и Search / Fetch API
```

### Пять понятий, без которых не обойтись

**Как работает MoE (смесь экспертов):**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T["Токен"] --> R{"Роутер"}
    R -->|"выбран"| E1["Эксперт 7"]
    R -->|"выбран"| E2["Эксперт 42"]
    R -.->|"спит"| E3["Эксперт 1…256"]
    SH["Общий эксперт"] --> O
    T --> SH
    E1 --> O["Выход слоя"]
    E2 --> O
```

> Вся модель хранится в памяти, но считается только малая часть. Поэтому MoE нужно **много памяти**, но **мало вычислений**.

| | Обычная (dense) модель | MoE-модель |
|---|---|---|
| Пример | R1-Distill-Qwen-32B | V4-Flash 284B |
| Считается на токен | все 32B | ~13B |
| Нужно памяти | под 32B | под 284B |
| Скорость генерации | как у 32B | как у ~13B |
| Где выгодна | одна мощная GPU | много RAM + GPU, Mac с большой памятью |

- **MoE (Mixture of Experts, смесь экспертов).** Модель состоит из множества «экспертов», но на каждый токен работает лишь малая часть. V4-Flash весит 284B, а считает как ~13B. Поэтому **памяти нужно много, а вычислений мало**, и для MoE хорошо подходит связка «много RAM + одна видеокарта».
- **Режим размышлений (thinking).** Сначала модель пишет рассуждение (` … `), потом ответ. Так она лучше решает математику, код и логику, но ответ получается медленнее и тратит больше токенов.
- **Дистиллят.** Маленькая модель (Qwen или Llama), дообученная на ответах большой R1. Все `deepseek-r1:1.5b…70b` в Ollama — дистилляты.
- **Квантизация.** Сжатие весов с 16 до 8/4/3/2 бит. Q4 примерно в 4 раза меньше FP16 и почти не теряет в качестве.
- **GGUF.** Формат файлов модели для llama.cpp, Ollama и LM Studio. Квант виден в названии файла: `Q4_K_M`, `Q8_0`, `IQ3_XXS`.

### Зачем запускать DeepSeek у себя

| Плюс | Почему важно |
|---|---|
| 🔒 **Приватность** | Код, договоры, медицинские данные не покидают твой компьютер |
| 💸 **Бесплатно** | Никакой оплаты за токены и подписок |
| 🌐 **Офлайн** | Работает в самолёте, в закрытом контуре, при блокировках |
| 🛠 **Контроль** | Свои системные промпты, параметры, дообучение |
| ♾ **Без лимитов** | Никаких «вы исчерпали лимит сообщений» |

**Минусы:** нужно хорошее железо, маленькие модели слабее облачных флагманов, настройка требует времени.
