# Open Lakehouse Compute Fabric (OLCF)

**An open-source lakehouse platform that extends Microsoft Fabric with Spark compute you own, and also runs completely on its own.**
Notebooks, SQL, pipelines and dashboards; a Spark fabric across your own machines; and **OLCF Intelligence**: discovery, lineage, a glossary and governance over everything it can see.

*Created and maintained by **[Justin Dodrill](https://github.com/jddevtime)**, a Microsoft Certified Technology Specialist and Database Administrator. Licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE).
Not affiliated with or endorsed by Microsoft; see [TRADEMARKS.md](TRADEMARKS.md).*

> **Status: 0.1.0 beta, for evaluation on trusted infrastructure.** It runs end to end on Linux and is covered by thousands of automated tests. [Status and maturity](#status-and-maturity) has the details, and the
> [release-readiness checklist](docs/development/release-readiness.md) lists what is still open.

**Jump to:** [What it is](#what-it-is) | [Three ways to run it](#three-ways-to-run-it) | [Extending Microsoft Fabric](#extending-microsoft-fabric) | [OLCF Intelligence](#olcf-intelligence-discovery-lineage-glossary-governance)
| [Runtimes](#spark-runtimes-fabric-13-and-20-compatible-side-by-side) | [Screenshots](#screenshots) | [Architecture](#architecture) | [Install](#install) | [Quickstart](#quickstart) | [AI and SI agents](#ai-and-si-agents-are-welcome)
| [Status](#status-and-maturity) | [Documentation](#documentation)

---

## What it is

OLCF gives you, on one laptop, a few on-premises machines, cloud VMs or Kubernetes:

* a **web console, REST API, CLI and Python SDK** with workspaces, lakehouses (Delta Lake, Iceberg discovery, Parquet), a SQL editor, dashboards, Jupyter-compatible notebooks, pipelines, environments, connections, secrets, schedules, alerts and administration;
* a **compute fabric**: every machine runs a small worker agent that connects *outward* to the control plane, and the enrolled machines together form a real Apache Spark Standalone cluster, with several immutable, signed Spark runtimes installed side by side;
* a **Microsoft Fabric compute extension**: one call in a Fabric notebook, `olcf.run_remote()`, sends the whole notebook to *your* Spark, which reads and writes OneLake directly and returns status, logs and the exit value to the Fabric cell and pipeline;
* **OLCF Intelligence**: it reads the platform (and, if you wish, a Fabric or Power BI tenant) to answer *what do we have, where does it come from, what depends on it, and who is responsible for it*, with a confidence on every lineage edge and every gap listed;
* an **MCP endpoint** so AI agents such as Claude Desktop and Claude Code can browse the catalog, follow lineage and run read-only SQL with exactly the permissions of the person who created the token.

Fabric is an adapter, not the core. Nothing in the platform needs a Microsoft subscription.

## Three ways to run it

| Mode | What you have | Needs | Start with |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Standalone** | the full platform on one machine: console, SQL on DuckDB, Python notebooks, dashboards, pipelines, Intelligence, MCP and a sample Retail lakehouse | Python only; **no Spark, no Fabric, no cloud** | `olcf quickstart` |
| **2. Multi-machine fabric** | the same plus a Spark Standalone cluster across several machines (servers, VMs, a rack, a cloud instance); several runtimes side by side; pools, queues, drain | a Spark runtime (`olcf runtime install --with-jdk`) and machines that can reach the control plane | `olcf worker enroll-token`, then `olcf-worker run` on each machine |
| **3. Fabric-extended** | Fabric notebooks and pipelines whose heavy compute runs on your own hardware, reading and writing OneLake directly | a Fabric tenant you control, the `olcf_fabric` wheel in a Fabric Environment, Entra and network set-up | [Fabric integration guide](docs/guides/fabric-integration.md) |

A single machine is the same design as a cluster of one: an embedded worker agent enrols itself with the control plane, so growing from mode 1 to mode 2 is adding machines, not migrating.

## Extending Microsoft Fabric

**How it works.**

1. In a Fabric notebook you attach the small, standard-library-only `olcf_fabric` package and call `olcf.run_remote()`.
2. The SDK sends the notebook as a **signed execution capsule** (HMAC-signed, single-use nonce) over HTTPS to your OLCF control plane. Nothing needs inbound access to your workers: they connect outward.
3. A deterministic **compatibility analyzer** (73 rules, shims for `notebookutils` and friends) checks the notebook first. Anything that cannot work on open-source Spark is rejected up front with the reason, not half-run.
4. The scheduler places the job on your Spark workers. Executors read and write **OneLake / ADLS Gen2 directly**; data never detours through the control plane.
5. Status, logs and the exit value stream back to the Fabric cell, and a Fabric pipeline's notebook activity sees the result like any local run.

**What it is good for:** running Fabric notebooks on hardware you already own, keeping heavy or sensitive compute inside your network, burst or batch work that should not consume Fabric capacity, development against a local copy of a lakehouse, and keeping a working path when Fabric is unavailable.

**What it is not:** it is not Microsoft's runtime and claims no parity with Fabric's proprietary optimisations (the runtimes are labelled *Fabric Runtime 2.0 Compatible* and *1.3 Compatible*). The assumptions behind the Fabric, Entra and OneLake integration, and an acceptance matrix you can run against your own tenant, are in [fabric-assumptions](docs/guides/fabric-assumptions.md).
Details: [the extension model](docs/concepts/fabric-extension-model.md), [the guide](docs/guides/fabric-integration.md).

## OLCF Intelligence: discovery, lineage, glossary, governance

Intelligence is a module layered over the platform's catalog. It answers **what do we have, where does it come from, what depends on it, who is responsible**, and it is deliberately honest about how sure it is.

* **Discovery.** Scans this installation and, optionally, a Microsoft Fabric / Power BI tenant (workspaces, lakehouses, tables and columns, notebooks, pipelines, semantic models, reports) or a saved Power BI scanner file. Scans are incremental, resumable and leased; a partial or failed scan never removes anything.
* **Lineage.** Pure, deterministic analyzers read SQL, PySpark/Python, notebooks, OLCF and Fabric pipelines, Spark job definitions, semantic models (TMDL, DAX, M), Power BI reports (PBIR) and scanner results, **without running your code**, and work out table-level and column-level lineage. The [support matrix](docs/reference/lineage-support.md) lists exactly what each analyzer understands.
* **Honest confidence.** Every edge carries its evidence and a level: `verified` (observed by a real run: jobs, notebooks and SQL publish `dataset.read / written / statement` events), `derived` (static analysis), `inferred` (matched by name or an assumed default) or `unknown`. What could not be seen is reported as a **gap** with the reason and the fix, never guessed.
* **Stable ids.** The same table is one asset (`ast_...`) whether it is named by an OLCF item, a Delta path, a OneLake path, a Fabric item id or a SQL name; the aliases are kept. Distinct tables that merely share a name are never merged.
* **Glossary and governance.** Business glossary, domains, data products, owners, classifications with a review queue and inheritance, certification, change requests, policies and a quality score. **Governance observes and reports; it does not enforce or block work in this release.**
* **Safe by design.** A failure in Intelligence never stops compute. Sampling column values is **off unless you turn it on**, per policy, with masking and a classified-column exclusion. Everything is available in the console, REST, CLI (`olcf intelligence`, `olcf governance`), SDK and MCP tools.

| | |
|---|---|
| Lineage of a report visual back through a semantic model and tables to the notebook that wrote them (the sample's report is synthetic) | Where does this come from: the origin of a column, with confidence on every step |
| Intelligence overview | Governance: ownership, classification review and certification |
| Impact analysis | Coverage and gaps |

Read more: [concepts](docs/concepts/intelligence.md), [user guide](docs/guides/intelligence.md), [lineage support matrix](docs/reference/lineage-support.md), [design decision](docs/adr/0017-intelligence-subsystem.md).

## Spark runtimes: Fabric 1.3 and 2.0 compatible, side by side

A **runtime** is an immutable, signed bundle: a Python environment with PySpark and every package pinned by hash, the Maven jars (Delta, Iceberg, S3, Azure) pinned by checksum, and an allow-list of the Spark settings a job may change. Several can be installed at once; the scheduler places a job only on a node where its runtime is ready.

| Runtime id | Family | Spark | Delta | Iceberg | Java | Scala | Python |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `olcf-rt-2.0.0` | `fabric-2.0-compatible` | 4.1.1 | 4.2.0 | 1.11.0 | 17 or 21 | 2.13 | 3.13 |
| `olcf-rt-1.3.0` | `fabric-1.3-compatible` (legacy) | 3.5.5 | 3.2.0 | 1.11.0 | 8, 11 or 17 | 2.12 | 3.11 |
| `olcf-rt-native-1.0.0` | `olcf-native` | 4.1.1 | 4.2.0 | 1.11.0 | 17 or 21 | 2.13 | 3.13 |
| `olcf-host-python` (built in) | `host-python`, no Spark | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | the worker's own Python |

* **Side by side.** Install and retire runtimes independently; a notebook, job or Fabric submission asks for a family (for example `fabric-1.3-compatible`) and runs only where that runtime is ready.
* **No Spark needed to start.** Python notebooks, DuckDB SQL, dashboards, Intelligence and MCP work on the built-in host-Python runtime; the Spark runtime (several hundred MB) is optional.
* **Signed.** Each manifest is Ed25519-signed. The bundled development key is public, so a production installation does not trust it until you re-sign with your own key ([hardening](docs/operations/hardening.md#6-supply-chain)).
* **Not Microsoft's runtime.** The versions follow what the open-source projects and Microsoft's public documentation list for Fabric Runtime 2.0 and 1.3. No parity with Fabric's proprietary optimisations is claimed.

More: [compute model](docs/concepts/compute-model.md).

## Screenshots

The console has light and dark themes, is served entirely from the package (no CDN, no remote fonts), and works at phone width.

**Notebooks.** A Jupyter-compatible editor on a real kernel running on a worker node; here the sample Python notebook after *Run all* (DuckDB, pandas and matplotlib, no Spark).

The Python sample notebook after Run all: a chart and a table produced on a worker node

**Home, Compute and Microsoft Fabric.**

| | |

| Home: fleet, cores, jobs, a guided checklist and a health strip | Compute: every machine with CPU, memory, disk and a lamp per component |
| Fabric integration: readiness checklist and a stepwise connection test | Runtimes installed side by side |

**SQL, lakehouse, dashboards, pipelines and AI agents.**

| | |

| SQL editor | Lakehouse explorer |
| Dashboard | Pipeline run graph with the critical path |
| Pipeline designer | MCP console: ready-to-paste configuration and a try-it box |

Dark theme example: [home](docs/images/ui/overview-dark.png), [notebook](docs/images/ui/notebook-python-dark.png), [lineage](docs/images/ui/intelligence-lineage-dark.png). More: [`docs/images/ui/`](docs/images/ui/).

### What is in the box

| Workspaces and items | multi-tenant workspaces; notebooks, lakehouses, SQL queries, pipelines, environments, Spark job definitions, variable sets, schedules, reports; versions, recycle bin, export/import, Git sync | [concepts](docs/concepts/workspaces-items-lakehouses.md) |

repositories.description: Never keep an agent waiting. A free, open-source Mac menu bar app for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor: see which session needs you and answer it with one keystroke.
repositories.readmeExcerpt:
Muster

   Never keep an agent waiting.
  A free, open-source Mac menu bar app for your Claude Code, Codex and Cursor sessions.

    Download for Mac   ·
   brew install --cask josefchen/tap/muster  ·
   agentmuster.app  ·
   Changelog  ·
   简体中文

  Two agents ask.  ⌥  ↓  shows why, two presses of  ⌥  ↩  answer them, and you never left what you were doing. Recorded from the app.

If you run a few coding agents at once, the slow part isn't the agents. It's noticing which one has been waiting on you for ten minutes. Muster sits in the menu bar, tells you the moment one needs you, and lets you answer without switching apps.

**See who needs you.**
A glass alert at the top of the screen the moment an agent waits on you. It stays until you answer.

**Answer from anywhere.**
Allow a command or pick an answer with  ⌥  ↩ , or right from the notification. The alert shows its keys.

**See why before you answer.**
 ⌥  ↓  unfolds the agent's reason, the whole command, or every option with its note.

**Your keys stay yours.**
Muster takes its keys only while something on screen needs them, and lets go while you type elsewhere.

** ⌥  Tab  to any agent.**
Most urgent first. Let go to land in its window, or the terminal it runs in.

**Find any session.**
 ⌃  ⌥  Space  searches the last three hours, with tokens and API-rate cost for each.

  Native AppKit and Liquid Glass · macOS 14+ · Apple silicon and Intel · no accounts or app analytics · MIT

## Install

**[Download Muster.dmg](https://github.com/josefchen/muster/releases/latest/download/Muster.dmg)** and drag it to Applications, or:

```bash
brew install --cask josefchen/tap/muster
```

macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon or Intel. Liquid Glass needs macOS 26.

## Answer prompts from Muster

Turn it on per agent in **Settings → Answer prompts from Muster**.

| | What you can answer |
|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Permission requests, multiple-choice questions, plan approvals |
| **Codex** | Approval requests (enable and trust the Muster hook in Codex Settings → Hooks, or `/hooks` in the CLI) |
| **Cursor** | Opens the prompt in Cursor |

The tour and Settings show each connection's progress. For Codex, Muster reads the client's hook status when supported, so a disabled, untrusted or changed hook stays pending. It never enables or trusts hooks on your behalf.

Use **Copy check prompt**, paste it into a local agent session that asks for approval, and answer the request from Muster. The connection is verified only when the request arrives, the answer is delivered, and the same session resumes in its transcript. The sample alert in the tour is practice and does not verify anything. Full access or automatic approval can skip this test because no permission request is made.

You can choose **Set up later** and use switching and search immediately. Unfinished answering setup remains visible in Settings and the menu. Verification records the last successful check, rather than a continuous connection: changed hooks require another check, and evidence older than a day is no longer marked current.

Muster adds one hook to the agent's own settings and removes exactly that when you turn it off. Beside the file it keeps `.muster-original`, the file as it was before Muster first changed it, and `.muster-backup`, the file before the latest change. A symlinked settings file stays a link, and a file Muster can't parse is left alone. Claude's native dialog stays live alongside Muster, and the first answer wins. If Muster isn't running, the agent asks as usual. Hooks talk to Muster on `127.0.0.1` with a per-install token.

## Shortcuts

| Keys | |
|---|---|
|  ⌥   Tab  | Switch. Tap to step, release to open, or click a row |
|  ⌥   ↩  ·  ⌥   ⌫  ·  ⌥   1 – 9  | Allow · deny · answer the prompt on the alert or in the switcher |
|  ⌥   ↓  ·  ⌥   ↑  | Unfold the alert's details · fold them |
|  ⌃   ⌥   Space  | Search every session |

Muster takes  ⌥  ↩ ,  ⌥  ⌫ , the arrows and the digits only while a prompt or the switcher is on screen, and lets go of them while you type in another app, so they keep working in your editor. Both shortcuts can be changed in Settings. Scripting: `muster://search`, `muster://next`, `muster://settings`, `muster://welcome`, `muster://whats-new`.

  Why not just a notification?

Claude Code can notify you on its own in some terminals, and a few lines of settings add a sound or a banner anywhere else; [this guide compares every option](https://agentmuster.app/guides/claude-code-notifications-mac). A notification tells you that something happened. With several sessions running you still have to work out which one, find its window and type the answer. Muster shows which one, answers it from where you are, and does the same for Codex and Cursor.

  How it works

Muster reads the session files each app already writes. Local sessions need no configuration.

| App | Read from |
|---|---|
| **Claude** (desktop, CLI, SSH sessions) | `~/.claude/projects` transcripts and Claude's session list |
| **Codex** (app and CLI) | `~/.codex/state_*.sqlite` threads and rollout logs |
| **Cursor** | The Agents window's chat list and agent transcripts |

Everything is opened read-only. File system events trigger a rescan, at most once a second; transcripts are read incrementally, only the bytes added since the last look.

**Remote sessions (1.4, in development).** Open **Settings → Remote sessions** and enable an SSH alias, or add `user@hostname`. Muster discovers explicit aliases from your SSH config without connecting; only enabled hosts are contacted. Each host needs Python 3 and noninteractive SSH access from this Mac. If SSH needs a password, a new host key confirmation or an unlocked key, connect in Terminal first.

The remote reader runs in memory and polls every three seconds. It reads recent Codex, Claude Code and Cursor data, then sends titles, project paths, status and question previews over encrypted SSH. Summaries stay in memory on the Mac. If a connection drops, the last summaries are marked offline while Muster reconnects. Search by host name to find its sessions.

Answer remote questions and permissions in the agent on that host. Codex links include the SSH host; other agents offer an SSH command to copy. Remote monitoring installs no permission hooks, so it can show only requests recorded in the agent's session data. It does not report remote token costs. The session list covers the last three hours, up to 500 sessions per host, and reports read failures or truncation in Settings.

  Cost estimates

Public list prices for the standard API tier, bundled and dated in Settings. Claude is priced message by message, including subagents, with 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes kept apart. Codex is priced from its running totals; OpenAI's long-context tier isn't applied, so Codex figures are a floor. Cursor records no token counts on disk.

Use your own prices from **Settings → Use my own prices…**, which writes `~/Library/Application Support/Muster/pricing.json`.

  Privacy

No accounts or app analytics. Optional SSH monitoring contacts only hosts you enable and transfers session summaries to this Mac; it does not copy full transcripts or raw tool payloads, forward your SSH agent, or install remote hooks. SSH keys and host trust remain managed by SSH. Host settings and read/unread timestamps keyed by session ID are saved on this Mac. Session titles, project paths and question previews stay in memory.

The update check asks GitHub for the latest release when you click Check for Updates, or once a day if you leave "Updates" on in the welcome tour (or tick it in What's New, or turn it on in Settings). The local prompt server listens on `127.0.0.1` only and needs a token that lives in your user defaults and the agents' hook settings.

The website keeps aggregate daily page-load and download-click counts, with no cookies or visitor identifiers. It honors Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control. See the [privacy page](https://agentmuster.app/privacy) and [measurement guide](docs/measurement.md).

  Build from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/josefchen/muster.git && cd muster
./build.sh            # build, install to ~/Applications, launch
./test.sh             # reader tests against fixture files
scripts/e2e.sh        # end-to-end: the real app against a fake home folder
```

`scripts/e2e.sh` drives the built app the way the agents and you would (transcripts, hook requests, the switcher, deck and alert) without touching your own agents or settings; `--soak [minutes]` checks CPU and memory under load, and `--ui` replays real keystrokes and clicks (it takes over the keyboard while it runs).

`scripts/release.sh  ` builds a universal, signed and notarized DMG and writes its GitHub release notes from [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md), and `scripts/site.sh deploy` publishes [agentmuster.app](https://agentmuster.app) and its changelog page to Cloudflare. `scripts/capture-stills.sh`, `scripts/record-scene.sh`, `scripts/record-answer.sh` and `scripts/tour.sh` regenerate the screenshots, the videos and the welcome tour from demo mode (`Muster --demo`). Muster opens and plays each scene itself, so they need Screen Recording and nothing else.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

  MIT License. Muster is independent and not affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI or Anysphere.

repositories.description: Cromford: the open-source software factory. Tickets in, reviewed, merged and production-checked changes out.
repositories.readmeExcerpt:
# Cromford

Cromford is the open-source software factory ([cromford.dev](https://cromford.dev)). It takes tickets off a product board,
decides which are actually ready to build, plans them, builds them on a remote
machine, reviews the result adversarially, opens a PR, QAs the preview, merges,
confirms the deploy rolled, and then checks in production that the thing it
merged is really there.

It runs unattended. The design problem it exists to solve is not "can a model
write code" — it is what has to be true around the model so that a loop nobody
is watching does not open the wrong PR, spend money twice, or tell a customer
something shipped when it did not.

## The pipeline

One ticket moves through fixed stages. Each has its own runner, its own model,
its own budget, and its own idea of what "done" means.

| Stage | Script | What it does | Refuses when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **triage** | `bin/run-triage.sh` | Reads the whole ticket thread and decides RUN or SKIP | The last word is a question to the customer that nobody answered |
| **plan** | `bin/run-build.sh` | Writes the change down first, ending in named acceptance tests | It cannot name a test that would fail today |
| **build** | `bin/run-build.sh` | Implements against the plan, on a watcher box or a Fly machine | Tests were weakened rather than made to pass |
| **review** | `bin/run-build.sh`, `bin/review-prs.sh` | An adversarial pass over the diff, never the author's own session | The verify script does not prove the behaviour it claims |
| **preview QA** | `bin/e2e-smoke.sh` | Loads the PR's own preview deployment and clicks | The route 404s or the preview never built |
| **merge** | `bin/merge-conductor.sh` (owner; observe-only until its flags), `bin/merge-queue.sh`, `bin/merge-sweep.sh` | Every harness PR sits in one named state with an age budget; queued per project so two builds never race the same base | CI is not green, the base moved, the head moved after the approval, or the tier is wrong |
| **deploy-verify** | `bin/deploy-train.sh` | Confirms a production deployment actually followed the merge | No deployment appeared within the window |
| **post-merge QA** | `bin/postmerge-qa.sh` | Drives the real production surface | The shipped behaviour is not there |

Stages talk through files and a database, not through one long conversation. A
stage that dies is restartable because its inputs are on disk.

**Merge tiers.** A build lands in tier 1 or tier 2. Tier 1 is eligible for
automatic merge once review approves and CI is green. Tier 2 waits for a human.
`flags/automerge-disabled` forces every build to tier 2 —
`bin/run-build.sh:1592`.

## What holds it together

**Deterministic before LLM.** Anything a script can decide, a script decides.
The gate that says "this ticket has an unanswered question on it" is a status
field and a comparison, not a judgement call — so it costs nothing, never
drifts, and is testable (`bin/triage-gate.sh`; on GitHub-Issues projects its
fingerprint also carries the open harness PRs, so a merge or a check flip
wakes the tick). The model is asked only the questions that genuinely need
reading comprehension.

**Configuration is data.** Which model a stage uses, what a lane may spend,
which projects are enrolled, what may run concurrently: rows and registry files,
not constants. `fleet.conf` is the project registry and no script keeps its own
copy — `tests/fleet-projects-not-hardcoded-test.sh` fails if one tries.

**A fleet of boxes, plus an optional pool.** Each project's watcher runs on a
box; `fleet.conf` column 6 says which. One box is the hub and runs the
cross-project lanes. Builds can optionally be pushed to an ephemeral Fly machine
per build instead of running on the watcher — opt-in, and nothing breaks if you
never enable it (`bin/fly-pool.sh`).

**Multi-vendor lanes.** Every stage names a runner. When the primary is missing,
unauthenticated, or fails, `bin/agent-call.sh` walks a fixed ladder —
claude → grok → codex-configured openrouter → fireworks — alerting as it
degrades, and refusing to walk it at all when the failure was a budget stop or a
kill. The order is pinned by `tests/agent-call-provider-order-test.sh`.

**Every call is priced.** `bin/agent-call.sh` appends a 16-column row to
`logs/cost.csv` for each call. `bin/cost-rows-push.sh` ships rows to D1 every 10
minutes; `bin/cost-rollup.sh` builds the per-PR view nightly. A model with no
price in `catalog/model-prices.json` raises a daily alert rather than quietly
costing $0.

**It learns from its own PRs.** Review findings are mined for repeats
(`bin/rule-miner.sh`), and a family of repeats becomes a guardrail under
`guardrails/` — a rule that fails next time in CI instead of being found again
by a reviewer. Nothing in that lane merges or loosens a gate; it only tightens.

## Run it on your own accounts

You can run Cromford on your own Cloudflare, GitHub, Fly (or VM) and model
accounts. Fork it, copy the settings template, fill it in, and check it:

```bash
gh repo fork  /  --clone
cp env-templates/selfhost.conf.example selfhost.conf
bin/selfhost-install.sh --config selfhost.conf --dry-run
```

The dry-run prints every resource, env line, spend cap and secret name, and
creates nothing. The installer's `--apply` step is not built yet, so resources
are still built by hand. [docs/SELF-HOST.md](docs/SELF-HOST.md) walks through
every setting, the caps, upgrades and the common failures.

## Read next

| If you want to | Read |
|---|---|
| Run it on your own accounts, from a fork | [docs/SELF-HOST.md](docs/SELF-HOST.md) |
| Stand up your own fleet, or join one | [docs/OPERATOR-SETUP.md](docs/OPERATOR-SETUP.md) |
| Recover a wiped box (Orgo snapshot + R2 state backup) | [docs/RESTORE.md](docs/RESTORE.md) |
| Make your app drivable by the harness | [docs/BOARD-API-CONTRACT.md](docs/BOARD-API-CONTRACT.md) |
| Contribute a change | [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) |
| Understand what a build actually does, step by step | [docs/RUN-BUILD-GRAPH.md](docs/RUN-BUILD-GRAPH.md) |
| Understand the database and who writes what | [docs/DB-COORDINATION-SPEC.md](docs/DB-COORDINATION-SPEC.md) |
| Understand how context is composed and budgeted | [docs/CONTEXT-COMPOSITION.md](docs/CONTEXT-COMPOSITION.md) |
| Make a lane advance on a GitHub event instead of its cron tick | [docs/EVENTS.md](docs/EVENTS.md) |
| Know which LLM account pays for what | [docs/ACCOUNT-ROUTING.md](docs/ACCOUNT-ROUTING.md) |
| Read what went wrong before, and what the rule is now | [docs/LESSONS.md](docs/LESSONS.md) |
| Run a factory day to day: what went wrong, the defaults, the knobs | [docs/OPERATING.md](docs/OPERATING.md) |
| Understand how this repository relates to Cromford | [docs/ABOUT.md](docs/ABOUT.md) |
| See the dated notes this README used to be | [docs/CHANGELOG-NOTES.md](docs/CHANGELOG-NOTES.md) |

Repeated procedures are repo-managed skills, one `SKILL.md` per competency under
[skills/](skills/), deployed to every box by `bin/sync-skills.sh`. A session
loads a tested procedure on demand instead of carrying it in every prompt.

## Verification contract

**Run the suite:**

```
for t in tests/*.sh tests/mc/*.sh; do bash "$t"; done
```

No network, no secrets, no fixtures to generate. Some suites need `jq`,
`semgrep` or `codegraph` and skip cleanly without them; CI sets
`CODEGRAPH_REQUIRED=1` and `SEMGREP_REQUIRED=1` to turn those skips into
failures (`.github/workflows/harness-ci.yml`).

**Load-bearing suites** — these encode decisions rather than mechanics, and a
failure in one is a design regression, not a flake:

| Suite | What it protects |
|---|---|
| `tests/fleet-projects-not-hardcoded-test.sh` | No script may keep its own copy of the project list |
| `tests/cron-fleet-parity-test.sh` | The registry and the committed crontabs agree |
| `tests/agent-call-provider-order-test.sh` | The vendor failover ladder is the order it claims |
| `tests/iron-law-guard-test.sh`, `tests/lane-fence-test.sh` | The act-time command fence still denies what it must |
| `tests/alert-loop-test.sh` | An alerting lane cannot alert about its own alerts |
| `tests/board-lane-loop-test.sh` | The triage lane corrects an app's automated board move at most once per ticket and commit, then alerts and stops (TK-135 loop) |
| `tests/evals-suite-test.sh` | A prompt change still makes the same triage decisions. It drives `tests/evals/run-evals.sh`, which the `tests/*.sh` glob does not reach on its own |

**Platform.** The suite is written for Linux. On anything else, run it in the
container. The runner lives in `bin/`, not `tests/`, so the loop above never
re-enters it:

```
bin/run-tests-in-docker.sh
```

That builds a small Debian image with the tools the suite needs and runs the
whole thing inside it. It is close to CI but not identical — CI additionally
installs `semgrep` and `codegraph` and sets `*_REQUIRED=1`, which turns two
clean skips into real checks. Measured on the tree this was written against:

| | pass | fail |
|---|---:|---:|
| Debian trixie (the container) | 121 | 3 |
| macOS 15, bash 3.2 | 96 | 28 |

Most of the macOS gap is `mapfile`, bash 3.2 syntax and GNU-coreutils flags —
the platform, not the code. Three suites fail in the container but pass in CI;
they are named in the script's header, and that header says plainly that their
cause is not yet understood rather than guessing at one.

The container needs Docker and network for the first build, so the "no network,
no secrets" claim above is about the suite itself, not about fetching an image.

**Before you push**, if you are contributing to this repository, also run
`bash tests/no-client-identifiers-test.sh`. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

repositories.name: qantrip
repositories.description: Open-source prompt launcher: press ⌃Q, type a short command, and a parameterized prompt lands in any app. Rust core, native macOS app, end-to-end encrypted sync.
repositories.readmeExcerpt:
Nekro Qantrip

   An open-source prompt launcher. Press  ⌃Q , type a few keys, and a complete prompt lands in whatever app you're using.

   Website  ·
   Try it in your browser  ·
   Download  ·
   中文

> **Qantrip** is pronounced like *cantrip* — the D&D spell you can cast again and again at no cost. The **Q** is the key you press to cast one. It is not a typo.

Press ⌃Q in a terminal, type r sec --scope=staged -s, preview the prompt, and press ⌘↩ to insert it

## Why

If you work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or a chat window all day, you retype the same instructions over and over: *review the staged changes, focus on security, don't edit files…* Snippet tools can paste fixed text, but real prompts need small variations every time.

Qantrip turns your prompts into **parameterized templates** you call with a short command:

```text
r security --scope=staged -s focus on the auth module
│ │        │              │  └ free text, appended verbatim
│ │        │              └ short flag (-s = --strict)
│ │        └ option with a value (prefixes work: --sc=st)
│ └ positional value for the template's main parameter
└ template name or alias
```

…and inserts the rendered prompt into the app you were using, without touching your clipboard history and without accidentally submitting multi-line text in a terminal.

## Features

- **Discoverable command line** — exact, prefix and fuzzy matching; inline ghost completion; type `--` to see every parameter;  ↩  inserts exactly what the preview shows and  ⇥  completes, so one keystroke is enough even with a typo.
- **See what you'll insert** — a live preview highlights exactly which lines each parameter and your free text changed.
- **Templates are Markdown files** — YAML front matter declares parameters (bool, enum, multi-select, string, number, text); the body is a [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja) template. Edit them in any editor, or in the built-in library with a form editor, live preview and validation.
- **Insertion that stays out of your way** — paste-based (terminals and AI agents won't treat newlines as  Enter ), your clipboard is restored afterwards and the prompt is marked transient so clipboard managers skip it. No Accessibility permission? It falls back to copy-only.
- **Built for AI coding agents** — 17 built-in templates in English and Chinese (review, fix, debug, test, refactor, commit, PR, …);  ⌘↩  expands Claude Code's collapsed `[Pasted text]` placeholder.
- **Keyboard first, mouse friendly** — every parameter chip is clickable, and clicks rewrite the command line, so mouse and keyboard always agree.
- **Local first** — search, rendering and insertion work offline. Optional sync is [end-to-end encrypted](docs/sync-design.md).

## Install

Download the DMG — [Apple silicon](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/macos-arm64) or [Intel](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/macos-x64) — open it and drag **Qantrip** into Applications. Requires macOS 14 or later.

Qantrip isn't notarized by Apple yet, so macOS blocks the first launch: open **System Settings → Privacy & Security** and click **Open Anyway**. Updates keep your permissions and templates.

**Windows:** download and run [the installer](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/windows-x64) (no admin rights needed; a portable [zip](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/windows-zip-x64) is also available), then press  Ctrl+Q . It isn't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may ask you to click **More info → Run anyway**. Requires Windows 10 2004 or later (x64).

**Linux (preview):** download the AppImage — [x64](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/linux-x64) or [ARM64](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/linux-arm64) — make it executable and run it, or install the [.deb](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/linux-deb-x64) / [.rpm](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/linux-rpm-x64) (ARM64: [.deb](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/linux-deb-arm64) / [.rpm](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/dl/linux-rpm-arm64)). Press  Ctrl+Q ; on GNOME and KDE (Wayland) the system asks you to confirm the shortcut, and the welcome guide lets you allow auto-paste once. Requires GTK 4.14+ and libadwaita 1.5+ (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 40 or later). See [docs/install.md](docs/install.md).

## Writing a template

Create `~/Library/Application Support/Qantrip/templates/review.md` (Linux: `~/.local/share/qantrip/templates/`):

```markdown
---
name: review
aliases: [r]
description: Code review
params:
  focus:
    type: multi
    positional: true
    choices: [security, performance]
  strict: { type: bool, short: s, description: Report every doubt }
---
Review the current changes.
{% if focus %}Focus on: {{ focus | join(", ") }}.{% endif %}
{% if strict %}List anything uncertain and give a confidence level.{% endif %}
{% include "_extra" %}
```

Qantrip reloads it automatically. A file with the same name as a built-in template overrides it. You can also create and edit templates in the built-in library:

Template library with form editor and live preview

The full format is described in the [input grammar](docs/input-grammar.md) and on the [website](https://qantrip.nekro.ai/docs#templates).

## Project status

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| macOS app (panel, grammar, templates, library, settings, onboarding) | ✅ English and Chinese |
| Online demo (core compiled to WebAssembly) | ✅ [qantrip.nekro.ai](https://qantrip.nekro.ai) |
| Sync server (Cloudflare Workers + D1, ciphertext only) | ✅ deployed |
| End-to-end encrypted sync | ✅ macOS, Windows, Linux — [design](docs/sync-design.md) |
| Command mode for creating templates in the panel | ✅ |
| Windows | ✅ Windows 10/11 x64 (installer or portable zip) |
| Linux | 🧪 preview (x64 / ARM64; AppImage, .deb, .rpm; GNOME, KDE Plasma, X11) |
| AI-assisted template editing | 📝 planned |

## Architecture

```text
┌──────────────────────────── core/ (Rust) ────────────────────────────┐
│ input grammar · template library · MiniJinja rendering · usage ranking │
└───────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
            │ UniFFI                 │ wasm-bindgen
┌───────────▼──────────┐   ┌─────────▼──────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ apps/macos (Swift)   │   │ website demo (WASM)     │   │ apps/cloud (Workers)     │
│ AppKit + SwiftUI     │   │ same parser, same       │   │ website · accounts ·     │
│ hotkey · panel ·     │   │ templates, in the       │   │ E2EE sync API (opaque    │
│ paste · library      │   │ browser                 │   │ ciphertext, D1 + R2)     │
└──────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────┘
```

Each platform gets a native shell over a shared Rust core rather than a cross-platform UI framework — see [decision D6](docs/decisions.md).

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`core/`](core) | Rust core: grammar, templates, rendering, usage ranking; built-in templates in `core/templates/` |
| [`core/wasm/`](core/wasm) | WebAssembly bindings for the website demo |
| [`apps/macos/`](apps/macos) | macOS app (Swift, SwiftPM — no Xcode project required) |
| [`apps/linux/`](apps/linux) | Linux app (Rust, GTK4 + libadwaita, links the core directly) |
| [`apps/cloud/`](apps/cloud) | Website and sync server (Cloudflare Workers, React Router, Hono, D1) |
| [`docs/`](docs) | Product requirements, input grammar, sync security design, decision log |
| [`scripts/`](scripts) | Build, packaging and signing scripts |

## Development

```sh
cargo test --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml     # core tests
scripts/build-macos.sh                          # macOS app (dev-signed)
cargo run --manifest-path apps/linux/Cargo.toml # Linux app (needs GTK 4.14+ / libadwaita 1.5+ dev packages)

```

Design documents in `docs/` are written in Chinese; code, comments and commit messages follow the language of the surrounding code. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Security

Sync is end-to-end encrypted: keys are generated on your devices, and the server only stores ciphertext it cannot decrypt. The threat model, key hierarchy and the metadata the server *can* see are documented in [docs/sync-design.md](docs/sync-design.md). Please report vulnerabilities privately — see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

repositories.description: Tiny, dependency-free autocomplete for zsh. Press space, get suggestions.
repositories.readmeExcerpt:
# spacue

**Inline dropdown autocomplete for zsh - one file, zero dependencies.**

Type a command, press space, and a dropdown of likely candidates appears right
under your prompt: `package.json` scripts for npm/pnpm/yarn/bun, git
subcommands and branches, Makefile targets, ssh hosts, running PIDs,
directories for `cd`, files for everything else. Opening or filtering the menu
keeps your input unchanged. Press Down to preview the first candidate, then
use the arrow keys to navigate,
Enter or Tab to insert, Enter again to run, Esc to dismiss. Frequently
accepted suggestions rise to the top, with extra weight for the current folder.

## How

spacue in action

## Why

Most completion tooling is either heavyweight - daemons, background services,
model hooks - or locked to a single editor. spacue is **a single ~53 KB zsh
file**: no daemon, no background process, no extra runtime to install.
It sits in your shell and makes the prompt you already use smarter.
The optional demo media in this
repository is not installed by the one-line installer.

## Install

### macOS & Linux (one line)

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/merdanturan/spacue/main/install.sh | sh
```

The installer copies `spacue.zsh` to `~/.spacue/` and adds one source line to
`${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zshrc`. Updates are validated before replacing the installed
file, so a failed download leaves your current installation intact.
From then on spacue loads automatically in **every** terminal
window, including the first one after every reboot - no login item, no
background daemon, nothing to start manually.

Open a new terminal window (or run `exec zsh`) and try `cd ␣`.

### Windows (WSL)

Native PowerShell/cmd has no zsh, so spacue runs inside [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install):

```powershell
wsl --install                                          # one-time, then reboot
wsl sh -c "sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y zsh" # one-time
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/merdanturan/spacue/main/install.ps1 | iex
```

Then open a new WSL terminal. `spacue_uninstall` or `uninstall.sh` removes
everything cleanly.

### Manual

```sh
git clone https://github.com/merdanturan/spacue "$HOME/.spacue"
echo 'source "$HOME/.spacue/spacue.zsh"' >> "${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zshrc"
```

### Plugin managers

```sh
antigen bundle merdanturan/spacue
zinit light merdanturan/spacue                       # zinit
git clone https://github.com/merdanturan/spacue \
  ~/.oh-my-zsh/custom/plugins/spacue                 # oh-my-zsh, then: plugins+=(spacue)
```

## Usage

| Key                | Action                                        |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `space`            | show suggestions without changing your input  |
| `↓`                | select the first item, then move down         |
| `↑`                | select the last item, then move up            |
| `Enter` / `Tab`    | accept the selected item, or the first if none is selected (does **not** run) |
| `Enter` (again)    | run the line                                  |
| `Esc` / `Ctrl+G`   | close the menu, keep what you typed           |
| keep typing        | filter suggestions, keeping your typed input  |

Lists taller than the terminal show a suggestion count until you press
Up or Down to browse them.

What shows up per command:

| Command                                  | Candidates                                    |
|------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `npm` / `pnpm` / `yarn` / `bun`          | `package.json` scripts (with the real command as hint) + subcommands; dependencies for `install`/`add` |
| `git`                                    | subcommands; branches & changed files per subcommand; remotes for push/pull |
| `make`                                   | Makefile targets (`## comment` shown as hint) |
| `ssh` / `scp` / `sftp`                   | hosts from `~/.ssh/config` + `known_hosts`    |
| `kill` / `killall` / `pkill`             | running PIDs / process names                  |
| `cd` / `pushd`                           | directories (including `../`)                 |
| `ls`, `cat`, `vim`, `code`, `grep`, ...  | files & directories                           |
| `ls -`, `curl -`, `git commit -`, ...    | common flags                                  |
| anything else                            | files & directories, including later arguments |
| `sudo` / `env` / `time` / `command` ...  | the wrapped command's own candidates          |

Fuzzy fallback: `npm run bi␣` still finds `build`.

Built-in providers supply command-specific suggestions for the commands above.
Other commands receive file suggestions; spacue does not bundle a full CLI
specification catalog. Plain Tab outside a spacue menu still uses your installed
zsh completions. Commands after `|`, `&&`, `||`, and `;` use their own provider.

## Configuration

Set these before spacue loads (or export them in `~/.zshrc`):

| Variable                 | Default | Meaning                                            |
|--------------------------|---------|----------------------------------------------------|
| `SPACUE_ENABLED`         | `1`     | master kill switch                                 |
| `SPACUE_HINTS`           | `1`     | show descriptions next to items                    |
| `SPACUE_GENERIC`         | `1`     | file candidates for unknown commands               |
| `SPACUE_NATIVE`          | `0`     | opt in to installed zsh completions for other commands |
| `SPACUE_FUZZY`           | `1`     | substring fallback when prefix matching is empty   |
| `SPACUE_TYPING_TRIGGER`  | `1`     | reopen the menu while typing after `dir/`          |
| `SPACUE_COMPINIT`        | `1`     | auto-load compinit when your setup lacks it        |
| `SPACUE_DISABLED`        | `()`    | providers to turn off, e.g. `SPACUE_DISABLED="ssh kill"` |
| `SPACUE_MAX`             | `200`   | max candidates in spacue's own provider menus       |
| `SPACUE_STATS`           | `1`     | rank by accepted suggestions; `0` disables reads and writes |
| `SPACUE_STATS_FILE`      | `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/spacue/stats.tsv` | local usage file |

## Native completions (opt-in)

To use installed zsh completion definitions for commands without a spacue
provider, set this before loading spacue:

```zsh
SPACUE_NATIVE=1
```

For example, `docker ␣` can use an already installed `_docker` definition.
Spacue does not install completion definitions or the commands themselves.
Built-in providers, registered custom providers and the existing path-command
behavior retain precedence. If a native definition produces no matches, the
ordinary file fallback is used when `SPACUE_GENERIC=1`.

Native groups retain zsh's filtering, ordering, descriptions, quoting and suffix
rules. They are not usage-ranked or subject to spacue's candidate cap; those
features continue to apply to spacue's own candidates. Enter/Tab acceptance and
Esc/Ctrl-G dismissal work the same way. Plain Tab remains unchanged.

This is disabled by default for compatibility. Like pressing stock Tab, calling
an installed completion function can execute programs and its latency depends
on that function. Set `SPACUE_NATIVE=0` to return to file-only fallback.

## Local ranking

Selections accepted with Enter or Tab are counted immediately, in the directory
where they were accepted. Merely previewing, typing, or dismissing a suggestion
does not count. The score is **global frequency + 2 × current-directory
frequency**; ties keep the provider's original order. Package scripts share
their counts between `npm ␣` and `npm run ␣` (likewise for other package managers).

The file uses TSV (`command:candidate`, count, directory) rather than JSON/TOML
so zsh can read it without an extra parser. An empty directory field holds a
global count. Records are capped at 8,000; writes use a lock and atomic rename
to protect updates from multiple terminals. File permissions are private to
your user. No command history, script body, or telemetry is collected; the file
contains accepted candidate names and directory paths. Names with tabs or
newlines are not recorded.

Set `SPACUE_STATS=0` to opt out. Remove the stats file to reset ranking, or set
`SPACUE_STATS_FILE` to a different path. Uninstalling the plugin preserves this
usage file; remove it separately to delete your learned rankings.

Parsed counts are cached in memory. Atomic updates from other terminals,
directory/file changes and the next prompt invalidate that cache. Within an
active menu, built-in provider candidates are reused before filtering and
before the display limit; new interactions refresh them. Custom providers
continue to run for every filter update.

## Custom providers

A provider is a zsh function that receives `(cmd token args...)`, appends
candidates with `spacue_add VALUE [DESC] [MATCH]`, and optionally sets
`SPACUE_KIND` to `words` or `paths`:

```zsh
# ~/.zshrc, after spacue loads
spacue_register docker _my_docker
_my_docker() {
  local cmd=$1 token=$2 sub=$3
  SPACUE_KIND=words
  case $sub in
    ('') for s in run build ps images pull push logs exec compose; do
           spacue_add "$s"
         done ;;
  esac
}
```

## FAQ

**Does it need macOS Login Items or a startup daemon?**
No - and it can't be one. A Login Item (or LaunchAgent) is for *processes* the
system starts at boot. spacue is not a process; it is code that runs inside
every zsh session. The `source` line in `~/.zshrc` is the persistence
mechanism: every shell you open - first thing after a reboot included - loads
it automatically. If spacue ever ran a daemon instead, it *would* show up as a
background item - which is exactly the kind of hidden baggage this tool exists
to avoid.

**Does it slow down my prompt?** Candidates are computed on demand and cached
(`git` 3 s, `ssh` 10 s, `ps` 2 s TTLs). If your shell has not loaded the zsh
completion system, spacue initializes it once; `SPACUE_COMPINIT=0` opts out.

**Does it break Tab?** Plain `Tab` keeps zsh's standard completion. While a
spacue suggestion is active, Tab accepts it just like Enter. Previous key
bindings are restored when the suggestion is accepted or dismissed.

**Known conflicts:** `fzf-tab` replaces the same menu machinery, so don't load
both.

## Compatibility

Requires zsh with its standard `complist`, `stat`, `system`, and `files` modules
(included with macOS and typical Linux/WSL zsh packages). Tested locally on
zsh 5.9. The JSON reader
for `package.json` prefers `node`, then `jq`, then `python3`, and finally falls
back to pure awk - no hard dependency.

## Development

Tests drive a real pty running zsh and assert on the rendered screen, plus
isolated cache, ranking, concurrency, quoting, and installer regressions.
No Python packages are needed:

```sh
python3 tests/run.py        # run the maintained suites sequentially
python3 tests/regression.py # fast non-PTY regressions
python3 tests/test_ui.py    # acceptance and quoting regressions
python3 tests/test_native.py # installed completion integration
python3 tests/benchmark.py   # warm filtering, synthetic large-directory workload
```

The benchmark uses 200 package scripts, 5,000 directories and 8,000 ranking
records. `--plugin /path/to/spacue.zsh` runs the same workload against another
version. Timings are measurements, not test thresholds; run benchmarks separately
from the test suites for a useful comparison.

[Recorded comparison and methodology](docs/performance.md).

The older `diag*.py` files outside the runner are exploratory diagnostics,
not additional release checks. The maintained PTY suites share fixtures and
must not be run in parallel.

## License

repositories.readmeExcerpt:
TwinDesk

   All your computers and your phone, working as one desk.
  Screens, apps, files, clipboard, notifications, mouse and keyboard, shared between Mac, Windows, Linux and Android.
  Free and open source.

    ⬇️ Download   ·
    Website   ·
    How it works

  A second Mac's screen in a window, the Mac's desktop extended onto a tablet, and the phone app. Every screenshot here is from the real app.

---

Your devices are good at their own jobs and bad at working together. TwinDesk fixes that.
Put a **Mac and a Windows PC** side by side and use them with one mouse and keyboard. Open the
PC's apps on the Mac. Turn an old laptop or your **Android tablet** into a second screen. Send a
file from your phone in two taps, and paste on one device what you copied on another.

- **Any combination.** Mac ↔ Windows, Mac ↔ Mac, PC ↔ PC, Linux ↔ anything, and Android ↔ any computer.
- **No account, no cloud.** Devices talk directly over your network or a USB cable, on an encrypted link.
- **No extra hardware, no root.** Install the app on each device and pair once.

### 💻 [Two computers, one desk](#-two-computers-one-desk)
One mouse and keyboard · second screen · the other computer's apps in windows · files and folders · clipboard · terminal · sound · notifications

### 📱 [Your phone and tablet join in](#-your-phone-and-tablet-join-in)
The phone's screen and apps in windows · tablet as a second screen · share menu on both sides · clipboard · notifications · Wi-Fi or USB

# 💻 Two computers, one desk

## 🖱 One mouse and keyboard for both

Push the pointer off the edge of your screen and **keep working on the other computer**, as if
they were one. Your keyboard follows the pointer. Trackpad gestures (Spaces swipes, pinch to zoom,
show desktop) carry over, and a double-tap of the hotkey brings everything home. Set which side the
other computer is on, edge resistance and pointer speed.

## 🖥 A second screen, or the other screen in a window

Extend your Mac onto a PC or another Mac with a **real virtual display**, or mirror it. Or bring
the other computer's screen into a window and control it from there. Low-latency H.264 with
*Fastest* and *Smooth* playback, and optional frame generation.

## 🪟 The other computer's apps, right here

Open a **Windows app on your Mac** (or a Mac app on your PC) and it gets **a window of its own**,
with its own Dock icon or Start-menu pin. No full remote desktop, just the app you need, next to
your own.

Pick any app from the other computer's list and it opens in a moment:

## 📁 Files, folders and a terminal

**Drag files across the screen edge** and drop them anywhere, or copy with  ⌃⌥C  and
paste with  ⌃⌥V  ( Ctrl+Alt+C/V  on Windows and Linux). Send from the macOS Share
menu or Explorer's *Send to*, or **share a folder** that shows up as a network drive on the other
side. Need a shell? `ssh twindesk` opens one on the other computer, no passwords needed.

## 📋 One clipboard

Copy on one computer and paste on the other, instantly or when you switch over. Entries from
password managers are skipped, and a Recent list keeps the last few things you copied.

## 🔔 Notifications, sound and more

See one computer's notifications on the other as native notifications, and hear one computer's
sound on the other. Wake a sleeping computer with Wake-on-LAN, and every switch you flip is
shared by both sides and remembered for the pair.

## 🤝 Mac and Windows, side by side

The same app on every platform, so a Mac and a PC pair just like two Macs. Here's a Mac connected to
a Windows PC, with the PC's apps ready to open on the Mac:

# 📱 Your phone and tablet join in

Most phone links stop at notifications and a file drop. In TwinDesk your Android phone or tablet is
a **full peer**: it pairs like a computer and gets the same features.

## Your phone, right on your desktop

See your phone's screen in a window and control it with your mouse, trackpad and keyboard. Better
still, open **single Android apps in windows of their own**, side by side with your desktop apps.
Pin them to the Dock or the Start menu and use them like any other app.

Every app on the phone is one click away from the computer's Phone page, along with its battery,
the connection and a button to bring up the whole screen.

## A second screen you already own

Turn a tablet or phone into an **extra monitor**. Choose **Extend** to get more desktop space, or
**Mirror** to show what's on your screen. Drag windows onto it, and use touch as the mouse: tap to
click, hold to right click, two fingers to scroll. Start it from the computer or from the tablet
itself.

## Sharing as easy as AirDrop

Share a photo or a document from **any Android app**: pick *Send to computer* or *Copy to computer*
in the system share menu. On the computer, use the **macOS Share menu**, **Explorer's Send to**, drag
files across the screen edge, or press  ⌃⌥C  /  Ctrl+Alt+C  to copy them and paste
them anywhere on the phone. Files arrive with a notification you can tap to open.

## Copy here, paste there

Copy text on your computer and paste it on your phone, or the other way around. It's instant, it
works in the background, and a Quick Settings tile sends the phone's clipboard with one tap.

## Your mouse and keyboard on the phone

Push the pointer past the edge of your screen and it **carries on onto the phone**. Type with your
real keyboard in any Android app, scroll with your trackpad, then double-tap the hotkey to come back.

## Notifications both ways

Your phone's notifications show up on your computer as **native notifications**, and the
computer's can show up on your phone. Hide the message text for privacy or mute single apps.

## Wi-Fi or USB cable, your choice

TwinDesk finds your phone on the network by itself and reconnects after a Wi-Fi drop. Plug in a
**USB cable** and it switches over for even lower latency (single-digit milliseconds), then back to
Wi-Fi when you unplug. The current link and its latency are always shown at the top of the app.

## Made for phones and tablets

The Android app adapts to the device: tabs at the bottom on a phone, a full sidebar on a tablet.
Every page names the computer you're connected to and shows what's shared in each direction.

You also get **Quick Settings tiles** (*Send clipboard*, *Wireless debugging*), **home screen
shortcuts** to the computer's screen, an ongoing notification with what's connected, and **sound**
in both directions.

# Get it

## Works with

| Pair | What you get |
|---|---|
| Mac ↔ Windows PC | Everything in *Two computers, one desk* |
| Mac ↔ Mac | Everything |
| PC ↔ PC | Everything |
| Linux ↔ Mac, PC or Linux | Everything ([a few differences](#linux)) |
| Android ↔ Mac, Windows or Linux | Everything in *Your phone and tablet join in* |

## Get started

1. **Download** TwinDesk for each computer and your phone from the [releases](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases).
2. **Open it on both.** They find each other on the same network (or over a USB cable for a phone).
3. **Pair once** by comparing a code. From then on they connect by themselves.

For the phone's screen, apps, touch and mouse, TwinDesk walks you through turning on Android's
wireless debugging once ([details](#wireless-debugging)). Files, clipboard and notifications work
right away.

## Privacy

TwinDesk only talks to devices you've paired with, directly over your own network or cable. There
are no accounts, no telemetry and no cloud relay. The only internet request is an update check
against GitHub's public releases, which you can turn off.

---

# Under the hood

Everything below is for the curious and for people building TwinDesk themselves.

## Linux

On Linux, TwinDesk runs on both X11 and Wayland. On Wayland, the mouse and keyboard go through
evdev and uinput (the Setup screen grants access once), and screens are captured through the
desktop portal. A few things work a little differently:

- **Shared folder.** Sharing uses Samba. The first time, one password prompt installs it if it's
  missing and adds a network-only account. The other computer's folder is connected with GVFS
  and shows in the file manager's sidebar.
- **Copy and paste files.**  Ctrl+Alt+C  copies what's selected in the file manager in
  front (or files you already copied), and  Ctrl+Alt+V  pastes into the file manager
  window in front (else Downloads). Right-click › *Send to* works in Nautilus, Nemo, Caja,
  Dolphin and Thunar.
- **Dragging files across the edge.** Files dragged in from the other computer are dropped into
  the folder under the pointer, or the desktop. On Wayland, they go to the file manager window in
  front. Dragging files out of Linux needs an Xorg session.
- **Extend.** On GNOME (Wayland) it uses Mutter's own virtual monitor; pick "Virtual remote
  monitor" when the desktop asks which screen to share. On X11 it switches on a spare output of
  the graphics driver (not available on NVIDIA's driver). That needs a small helper, which the
  .deb installs; with the AppImage, Share screen › *TwinDesk virtual display* › Install puts it in
  once, with your password.
- **Apps.** Opening this computer's apps on the other side needs an Xorg session.
- **Android phone.** Everything in [Android](#android-in-detail) works on Linux too: the phone's screen and
  apps in windows, the mouse and keyboard across the edge, files, clipboard, notifications and
  sound. The package carries adb; the Setup screen's firewall fix opens mDNS (5353/udp) so the
  phone's wireless debugging is found.

## Android in detail

Install TwinDesk on the phone, open it next to TwinDesk on the computer and pair from Overview › Nearby. The phone needs Android 10, and Android 11 for everything that goes through wireless debugging.

### The phone app

The app is laid out like the computers' (a sidebar on tablets, tabs at the bottom on phones), and
every page names the computer it's connected to:

| Page | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Overview** | The computer you're connected to, Connect and Disconnect, nearby computers to pair with, and the wireless debugging card until that's set up |
| **Screen** | Use the phone as a screen for the computer: Mirror, or Extend the desktop onto it. Touch works as the mouse (tap to click, hold to right click, drag to select or move windows, two fingers to scroll), with the computer's sound and Smooth playback |
| **Cursor** | The computer's mouse on the phone across the screen edge, its pointer speed here, reverse scrolling, right and middle click |
| **Keyboard** | The computer's keyboard types on the phone, every key as a key, so any layout works and the soft keyboard stays out of the way. A keyboard on the phone types on the computer |
| **Clipboard** | Copy on one, paste on the other, each way on its own switch, at once or when sent |
| **Notifications** | The phone's notifications on the computer, with the text hidden if you like, and the computer's on the phone |
| **Files** | Send files, copy them to paste on the computer, and see where the computer's files land |
| **Sound** | The phone's sound on the computer, and the computer's sound on the phone |
| **General** | The phone's name, background running, and the permissions TwinDesk uses, each with its switch |
| **About** | Source code, releases, the license, and what goes over wireless debugging and the network |

And outside the app:

- **Share sheet:** *Send to computer* and *Copy to computer* in every app's Share menu.
- **Quick Settings tiles:** *Send clipboard* and *Wireless debugging*.
- **Home screen shortcuts:** the computer's screen, and wireless debugging on in one tap.
- **The ongoing notification** shows what's connected, with Exit.
- **Copied on the computer:** files copied with  ⌃⌥C  /  Ctrl+Alt+C  arrive as a
  notification with Copy (paste them in any app) and Save.
- **The computer can install the full app** over wireless debugging (Phone page › Notifications
  from the phone): Play Protect blocks downloaded apps

repositories.description: Run many AI agents at once on your Mac, about three times faster.
repositories.readmeExcerpt:
Locals

   Run many AI agents at once on your Mac, about three times faster.
  OpenCode, OpenHands, Cline, Aider and any OpenAI or Ollama app, on one local
  server built for many agents working at the same time.

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/main/install.sh | sh
locals code ~/my-project
```

That is all. The first time, Locals downloads a model that suits your Mac
(about 3 GB), starts it in the background and opens the OpenCode assistant in
your project. Nothing leaves your computer.

## What it is

Locals runs AI models on your own Mac and makes them fast when many requests
arrive at the same time. That is how today's AI agents work: a coding assistant
runs several helpers in parallel, and a team of agents can work on one task
together. Locals answers these requests together, and computes such a group of
requests far more efficiently on your Mac's graphics chip, so the whole team gets
its answers about three times faster than with the standard way of running
models on a Mac.

It works with the coding assistants you may already use, such as OpenCode,
Cline, Aider and OpenHands, and with any app or program that talks to OpenAI or
Ollama. Everything stays on your computer.

Locals is built on the paper
[Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09139)
(Arip Asadulaev, 2026). The paper goes below the classical memory bound of
Savitch's theorem for finding paths in the kind of graph that describes a JSON
format or a tool call, and turns this into an inference engine: text the format
already decides is written without running the model, the checks run on the
graphics chip, and a format needs about 3 MB of memory instead of up to 1.5 GB.
The full results are in the paper, among them sixteen tool-calling agents
finishing 2.5 times sooner than with mlx-lm and llguidance.

## Why Locals

Coding assistants no longer send one request at a time. OpenCode, OpenHands and
Cline run helpers in parallel, and teams of agents split one task between them.
On a Mac, the standard way of running models, mlx-lm, answers such requests
together but barely gets faster when there are more of them: it writes 87 tokens
per second for four requests and the same 87 for eight, so every agent you add
slows the others down. Locals keeps getting faster as requests are added, so the
more agents you run, the more it gives you. It is also faster for a single agent
at work, after a restart, and in long conversations:

| On a MacBook Pro with an M2 Pro and 16 GB, Qwen3.5-4B | Without Locals | With Locals | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 requests at once | 87 tokens/s (mlx-lm) | 271 tokens/s | 3.1x |
| 8 agents asking at once: time to the first word | 42 s (Ollama) | 1.6 s | 26x sooner |
| One agent rewriting a 100-line file | 43 tokens/s (mlx-lm) | 128 tokens/s | 3.0x |
| An agent's first request after a restart | 16 s (mlx-lm) | 1.7 s | 9.6x sooner |
| A follow-up question about a 48,000-token document | out of memory (mlx-lm) | 0.6 s | |
| 16 coding agents calling tools (Qwen3.5-2B) | 75 s (mlx-lm) | 29 s | 2.5x |
| 40 programming problems from LiveCodeBench, 8 at a time | 20 min (mlx-lm) | 8 min | 2.5x |

With 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 requests at once, Locals writes 64, 116, 160, 271 and 341
tokens per second, and mlx-lm 61, 82, 87, 87 and 157; a plain answer alone, with
nothing to reuse, comes at about the same speed. A token is roughly a word piece.
Ollama answers this model one request at a time, so the eighth waits for the other
seven; Magnitude's first word came after 16 s. A file rewrite is faster even alone
because the reply repeats the file, and Locals checks pieces of it taken from the
prompt in the same pass as the next word. After a restart, Locals reads the
agent's long system prompt from disk instead of again. On an M2 Max with 96 GB,
eight requests at once get 403 tokens per second from Locals and 152 from mlx-lm,
and bigger models gain more: 3.0x for Qwen3.5-9B and 3.1x for a 27B model. How
each number was measured:
[Ollama and Magnitude](https://github.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/blob/main/docs/measurements/README.md#against-ollama-and-magnitude),
[mlx-lm's own server](https://github.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/blob/main/docs/measurements/README.md#against-mlx-lms-own-server),
[the M2 Max](https://github.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/blob/main/docs/measurements/m2-max.md).

- **Many agents in the time of a few.** Eight agents working at once finish in
  about the time two would need one after the other, and the answers are the
  same as mlx-lm's.
- **Each turn picks up where the last one ended.** Locals keeps every
  conversation between turns, and long system prompts on disk across restarts,
  so an agent's next turn reads only what it added. With four agents in long
  conversations, 83% of what they sent came from memory, and a follow-up
  question about a 138,000-token document started in 2.4 seconds instead of
  eight minutes of reading it again.
- **Tool calls that always parse.** Replies are written in the model's own
  tool-call format under a grammar, so only the tools an agent offers can be
  called, and a reply cut off by its length limit still closes its call. A small
  model can also repeat itself or call the same tool forever; Locals notices and
  stops both.
- **A team of agents for bigger tasks.** `locals run` splits a task into parts,
  gives each part to several agents at once, each in its own copy of your
  project, and lets your tests decide. On four tasks that each span several
  files, it passed all eight attempts in about three minutes each; one agent
  alone passed four of eight in about five minutes each.

**How.** mlx-lm's way of multiplying by the model's compressed weights gets almost
no faster per request for the handful of requests at a time that agents send.
Locals uses GPU code written and tuned for exactly these small groups, and on M1
and M2 chips computes in a number format the chip handles natively.
[Why Locals is faster](https://github.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/blob/main/docs/why-faster/README.md) measures each difference on its
own, and [Measurements](https://github.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/blob/main/docs/measurements/README.md) has every benchmark and how
to repeat it.

## Works with your agents

Locals works with the coding agents and assistants people already use, on a
model running on your Mac. Each of these was tested end to end with Qwen3.5-4B
on a 16 GB Mac, on real tasks such as writing a program, running it and
reporting what it printed. One command starts Locals and connects the tool to it:

| Tool | Run |
|---|---|
| [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) | `locals launch hermes` |
| [Kilo Code](https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode) | `locals launch kilo` |
| [OpenCode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) | `locals code ~/my-project` |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | `locals launch openhands` |
| [Cline](https://github.com/cline/cline) | `locals launch cline` |
| [Aider](https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider) | `locals launch aider` |
| [Roo Code](https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code) | in VS Code, the settings from `locals launch editor` ([how](#use-it-in-apps-and-editors)) |
| [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) | `locals launch openclaw` |
| [Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code) | `locals launch claude` (through Anthropic's Messages API, which Locals also answers) |

`locals launch list` shows every tool it can open. Locals keeps running in the
background after you close a tool: `locals status` shows what it is doing and
`locals stop` stops it.

These tools rarely send one request at a time. They run subagents and helpers in
parallel, and several sessions can work at once; Locals answers all of them
together in one batch, which is where it is fastest. Most of them also start
every session with a long system prompt of 3,000 to 16,000 tokens. Locals reads it
once and keeps it, on disk too, so the next turns and the next sessions start
without reading it again, even after a restart.

 The logos belong to their projects and are shown only to say that Locals
works with these tools.

## Getting started

You need a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or newer) and macOS 14 or newer. A Mac
with 16 GB of memory gives the best results; with 8 GB, use one of the smaller
models.

Open the Terminal app and run:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/main/install.sh | sh
```

Then start a coding assistant on one of your projects:

```bash
locals code ~/my-project
```

The first time, Locals downloads a model that suits your Mac (about 3 GB),
starts it in the background and opens the OpenCode assistant in your project.
From then on it starts in seconds. If you already use the uv package manager,
you can install with `uv tool install git+https://github.com/Generated-Computers/Locals`
instead.

## Examples

**Work on a project with an assistant.** This opens OpenCode in your project, where
you can ask for changes in plain words and watch it read, edit and test your code:

```bash
locals code ~/my-project
```

**Give it one task and get the result.** The assistant does the task from start
to finish without opening a window, and prints what it did:

```bash
locals code ~/my-project --run "add a --verbose flag to cli.py and run the tests"
```

**Let a team of agents do a bigger task.** Several agents work on the parts of
the task at the same time, each in its own copy of your project, and your tests
decide when it is done. Your project is changed only when the tests pass:

```bash
locals run "write wordcount.py with a function count_words(text) and tests in test_wordcount.py" \
    --dir ~/my-project --check "python3 -m pytest -q"
```

**Ask a question about your code.** An agent reads the project and prints the
answer:

```bash
locals run "Which function parses dates, and which format does it expect?" --dir ~/my-project
```

**Chat with the model** in the Terminal, like a private chatbot:

```bash
locals chat
```

**Turn text into structured data.** Describe the fields you want in a JSON schema,
for example in a file called `person.json`:

```json
{"type": "object",
 "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}, "age": {"type": "integer"}, "email": {"type": "string"},
                "status": {"enum": ["pending", "approved", "rejected"]}, "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}},
 "required": ["name", "age", "email", "status", "tags"]}
```

Then the answer always follows it, field by field:

```bash
locals generate --prompt "Ana Silva, 29, ana@example.com, application approved, tags: vip, early" \
    --schema person.json
```

```json
{"name":"Ana Silva","age":29,"email":"ana@example.com","status":"approved","tags":["vip","early"]}
```

## Use it in apps and editors

Start Locals once with the model you want; it keeps running in the background:

```bash
locals start --model qwen
```

**The OpenCode app.** Run `locals setup --model qwen` once, then choose Locals in
OpenCode's model list. This works in the desktop app, the editor extension and
the Terminal version alike.

**Kilo Code, Cline and Roo Code in VS Code**, and **Continue, Zed and JetBrains.**
Choose the provider called "OpenAI Compatible" and enter these values. Run
`locals launch editor` to print them for the model that is running.

| Setting | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Base URL | `http://127.0.0.1:8321/v1` |
| API key | any text, for example `local` |
| Model | the model's name from the table below, for example `locals/qwen3.5-4b` |
| Context window | the number `locals launch editor` prints, if the extension asks for it |

**Apps that work with Ollama**, such as Open WebUI or Raycast, need no settings:
run `locals launch ollama`.

# jailed-claude

> Run [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/) inside an isolated Docker sandbox — switch **LLM-provider profiles** with a single keystroke, keep your history intact, and optionally **cut the network off**.

Docker
Shell
License

## 🚀 Quick Start

Just run the following commands:

```bash
# 1. Download only the installer and execute it
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RiccardoNocita/Jailed-Claude/master/install.sh | bash

# 2. Run (Wait only first time for image build)
jailed-claude
```

## What it is (and isn't)

`jailed-claude` is a thin **wrapper** around the official Claude Code CLI. It does **not** modify, patch, rebrand, or change how Claude Code thinks or behaves — the agent stays 100% stock. What it adds is a layer of *control and isolation* around it:

- **Sandboxing** — every session runs in a throwaway Docker container that can only see the folder you're working in (plus your Claude history).
- **Provider profiles** — you decide *which LLM provider / endpoint / model* Claude talks to, using small `conf/*.conf` files. Swap providers without touching anything else.
- **Optional network lockdown** — with `--isolated`, all traffic to the upstream provider (Anthropic) is blocked, so your code never reaches the cloud and nothing can phone home or auto-update.

> In short: same Claude Code, different cage. You pick who it talks to — and whether it's allowed to talk at all.

## Features

- 🐳 Isolated `docker run` on demand (no long-lived containers). Can't access files outside the trusted dir by mistake (Finally...)
- 🔌 Pluggable LLM-provider profiles via `conf/*.conf` (endpoint + auth + models)
- 🧠 History & config preserved: only `~/.claude/` and `~/.claude.json` are bind-mounted
- 🎯 Interactive model picker (fuzzy with [fzf](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf), numeric fallback) — `default` lets Claude decide
- 🔒 Isolated mode that blackholes the upstream domains (privacy / no telemetry / no auto-updates)
- 🛡️ Hardened container: drops all capabilities, `no-new-privileges`, runs as your UID/GID
- ⌨️ Ctrl+C aborts any prompt; non-interactive friendly via env overrides
- 📦 One-line remote install

## How the sandbox works

| Aspect | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Working dir | Your current folder is bind-mounted at the **same path** inside the container |
| Home | Only `~/.claude/` and `~/.claude.json` are mounted — nothing else in `$HOME` is exposed |
| User | Runs as your host UID:GID (no root, no stray files) |
| Capabilities | `--cap-drop=ALL`, `--security-opt=no-new-privileges`, `--init` |
| Host reachability | `host.docker.internal` mapped to the host by default (for local gateways) — disable with `JAILED_ALLOW_INTERNAL=0` |
| Image | Built on first run from `Dockerfile.jailed-claude` (`node:20-slim` + Claude Code + git/ripgrep/bash) |
